TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE TO THE ENGLISH EDITION

Bread of Eternal Life and Chalice of Everlasting Salvation is the English translation of Pan de Vida Eterna y Caliz de Eterna Salvación (IVE Press 2011); Bible quotations are taken from the New American Bible, Revised Edition, and liturgical texts follow the 3rd Edition of the Roman Missal. We have translated all of Saint Thomas Aquinas’s texts from the Latin; however, these English translations have been made in light of Fr. Buela’s Spanish translations, in an effort to maintain the emphasis of his interpretations.

After publishing her German translation of Saint Thomas’s De Potencia, Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein) made a remark that aptly applies to our efforts here: “No one could be more convinced than I am that others would have been better qualified for this work. Perhaps I would have been unable to summon the courage for it had I been aware of all the difficulties beforehand. Nevertheless, I consider it almost a miracle that the work was completed and that, in spite of all its deficiencies, it turned out as it did, for it came from hours snatched out of a full school schedule and a number of other obligations.”

I hope this translation is intelligible; I am, of course, solely responsible for its flaws.

The author dedicated this book to “the happy memory of John Paul the Great,” a dedication which I am more than pleased to reaffirm. Through his intercession, may this book lead many to discover the beauty and relevance of the Eucharist which, in the words of Saint Madeline Sophie Barat, “is paradise on earth!”

November 17th, 2012 Memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Hungary

INTRODUCTION

“Sacred Scripture laments the conduct of certain priests who, ‘despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, did not occupy themselves with the offices of the altar.’ 1

[2 Macc 4:14].”

SAINT THOMAS

With the goal of giving some talks about the Eucharist for the Spiritual Exercises for priests, given that it was the “Year of the Eucharist,” the thought occurred to me that I should cover the essential elements of Saint Thomas’s treatise on the Eucharist in the Summa Theologica and other works.

It was a sort of oblique foray into the questions about the Eucharist, eleven of them in total, which constitute something like the Gothic ribs of the “cathedral” of the Summa on the topic.

I chose different theological terms with the computer’s search engine, looking in that treatise for the words according to the topic that I wanted to develop, in order to see the Doctor’s use of those terms.

Later, I was encouraged to write this small book. I think that what is most important to the topic is found in chapters 7, 9, and 14. Perhaps, in another edition, I will expand the work with other terms.

I accept in advance any correction that the Church would want to make of my work, keeping in mind Aquinas’s illustrious example in the monastery of Fossanova: “The Abbot Theobald himself brought the Eucharist to him. Before receiving Communion, Thomas said in the presence of the ‘whole community of monks and many Dominicans and Friars Minor’ many ‘beautiful things’ concerning his firm belief in the real presence, and in particular this: ‘I have taught and written much on this most holy Body and on the other sacraments, according to my faith in Christ and in the holy Roman Church, to whose judgment I submit all my teaching.’”2

This work is intended as an acknowledgment of the Angelic Doctor, who is also called the “Eucharistic Doctor,” and of the Second Vatican Council. Forty years ago, on

October 28 , 1965, that Council became the first Ecumenical Council to recommend a theologian nominatim through the solemn proclamation of His Holiness Paul VI which promulgated the Decree Optatam totius, On Priestly Formation, and the Declaration Gravissimum educationis, On

Christian Education. These documents recommend Saint Thomas Aquinas, inviting us to place ourselves “under his guidance.”3

CONTAINS

“. . . Christ, who is the Holy of Holies.”4

SAINT THOMAS

Saint Thomas uses the Latin word continet (contains) and its derivatives over 100 times in his Summa Theologica. With this insistence, he clearly indicated the substantial difference that exists between the Eucharist and the other sacraments. The Eucharist contains Christ.

The Eucharist contains something sacred absolutely: Christ Himself. “A sacrament is called such because it contains something sacred. Something can be sacred in two ways: in absolute, or in relation to something else. This is precisely the difference that there is between the Eucharist and the other sacraments that have sensible material: while the Eucharist contains something sacred absolutely, namely, Christ Himself, the water of Baptism, however, contains something sacred by its relation to something else, that is, the power to sanctify. The same happens with the chrism and the other sacraments.”5 “It is called ‘the Eucharist,’ that is, ‘good grace,’ because ‘the grace of God is eternal life’ [Rom 6:23], or because it really contains Christ, who is ‘full of grace’ [Jn 1:14].”6

It is called a “host” because it contains Christ: “This sacrament is called a ‘sacrifice’ insofar as it represents the Passion of Christ. It is called a ‘host,’ insofar as it contains Christ Himself, who is ‘a sweet sacrifice,’ as is said in the Letter to the Ephesians [5:2].”7

Christ Himself is really and truly present in the Eucharist: “It cannot be known through the senses that Christ’s true Body and Blood are in this sacrament, but rather only through faith, which rests on the Divine Authority. Thus, regarding Luke 22, [19] ‘This is my body, which will be given for you,’ Saint Cyril says, ‘Do not doubt that this is true, but rather receive in faith the words of the Savior who, because He is Truth, does not lie.’

This is fitting, first of all, in the perfection of the New Law. The sacrifices of the Old Law contained the true sacrifice of Christ’s Passion only in figure, according to what the Letter to the Hebrews says [10:1], ‘the law has only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of them.’ It was fitting, then, that the sacrifice of the New Law, instituted by Christ, should have something more. It should contain the very Christ who suffered, and not only in meaning or figure, but rather in truth.”8

This is what we must first and principally consider when we consider the Eucharist’s effect on man: “First and principally, the effect of this sacrament should be considered from what is contained in it, which is Christ. Christ, when He came visibly into the world, brought with Him with life of grace, according to what is said: ‘grace and truth came through Jesus Christ’ [Jn 1:17]. So, too, as He comes to man sacramentally, Christ affects the life of grace in man, according to what is said, that ‘the one who feeds on me will have life because of me’ [Jn 6:57]. Thus Saint Cyril says ‘By uniting Himself with His own flesh, the Life-giving Word of God made it life-giving as well. It was fitting that He would unite Himself to our bodies through His Sacred Flesh and His Precious Blood, which we receive in a life-giving blessing in the bread and wine.’”9

Christ has infinite power in this sacrament-sacrifice: “the power of Christ contained in this sacrament is infinite. . . .”10

It contains the greatest good: “This sacrament, which contains Christ, is one of the greatest goods.”11

For this reason, we must show great reverence to “the sacrament which contains Christ in truth, and not only in figure.”12

It brings us to the glory of heaven because it contains Christ: “In this sacrament we can consider both the One from whom the effect proceeds, namely, Christ who is contained in it, and His represented passion. . . . This sacrament is concerned with leading to the attainment of eternal glory on account of both things. Christ Himself opened the doors to eternal life for us through His passion, as the Letter to the Hebrews reads: ‘He is mediator of a new covenant so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance.’ [Heb 9:15] Thus, the form of the sacrament says, ‘This is the chalice of My Blood, of the New and Eternal covenant.’”13

Christ is contained in the Eucharist in order to be spiritual food: “Christ is not contained in this sacrament in His proper species, but rather in sacramental species. Now, to eat spiritually can be done in two ways. . . . The second way of spiritually consuming Christ is to do so under the sacramental species, believing in Him with the desire to receive this sacrament. Not only is this spiritually consuming Christ, but also spiritually consuming the sacrament, which the angels cannot do. Thus, even if the angels spiritually consume Christ, they cannot, however, spiritually consume this sacrament.”14

It was fitting that the Eucharist be instituted at the Last Supper so that Christ could be in it: “This is so firstly on account of what this sacrament contains: Christ Himself is contained in it sacramentally. . . . Accordingly, Eusebius says, ‘As the Body that Christ had assumed would be taken from their eyes and raised to the heavens, it was necessary that He would consecrate the Sacrament of His Body and His Blood for us that day of the Last Supper, so that the One who once offered Himself as our ransom might be forever adored in mystery.’”15 “Secondly, it is fitting because, as the Apostle says, no one can be saved without faith in Christ’s passion: ‘whom God set forth as an expiation, through faith, by his blood.’ [Rom 3:25] So it was fitting that at all times men might have some representation of the Lord’s Passion. In the Old Testament, the special sacrament was the paschal lamb, and so the Apostle writes, in 1 Cor 5 [7], ‘Our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.’ In the New Testament, the Eucharist succeeds the lamb, because, as the lamb was a figure of the future, the Eucharist is a remembrance of the past passion. So, it was fitting that, as His Passion was imminent and the old sacrament had been celebrated, Christ would institute the new sacrament, as Pope Leo says.”16

Christ is entirely present, totally present: “under the species of bread, by means of the sacrament, not only is the flesh of Christ contained, but rather the entire Body of Christ, that is, bones, nerves, etc;”17 “in this sacrament the entire Christ is contained.”18

The Eucharist is the sacrament of the Passion, because it contains Christus passus: “The Eucharist is the perfect sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, in as much as it contains Christ Himself who has suffered.”19 “Insofar as it is Christ who has suffered [Christus passus] who is contained in this sacrament.”20 “It was fitting, then, that the sacrifice of the New Law, instituted by Christ, should have something more. It should contain the very Christ who suffered, and not only in meaning or figure, but rather in truth.”21

Christ becomes present by conversion: “Christ begins to be in this sacrament by the conversion of the bread and the wine.”22

Let us therefore affirm that the Eucharist is the sacrament in which “there are truly, really, and substantially contained the Body and Blood together with the soul and divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and therefore the whole of Christ.”23

CHANGE

The words of the change of the bread and wine 24

“are as if Christ were present saying them.”

SAINT THOMAS

Our Lord’s Body and Blood become present under the appearances of bread and wine by the change of the entire substance of the bread and of the wine into the entire substance of Christ’s Body and Blood. This admirable change receives the name of transubstantiation.

The Angelic Doctor teaches that it is not by local movement that Christ becomes present in this sacrament, but rather by a change of substance: “Some have said that the substance of bread and wine remain in this sacrament after the consecration; however, this position cannot be sustained. First of all, this is because this position takes away the truth of the sacrament, as it belongs to the truth of the sacrament that Christ’s Body truly exists in it; it was not there before the Consecration. Now then, a thing becomes present where it was not before either by local movement or by the change of something else into it, just as a fire starts in a house because it is brought there or because it is produced there. It is clear, though, that Christ’s Body does not begin to be in this sacrament because of a local movement. First, this is because it would follow that Christ would cease to be in heaven, because anything that moves locally cannot reach a new location without leaving the place it was at before. Secondly, every body that moves locally must pass through all the spaces in between, and that cannot be said here. Thirdly, it is impossible for one locally moving thing to end up at different places at the same time, which happens when Christ’s Body begins to be in many places at the same time in this sacrament. For these reasons, Christ’s Body cannot begin to be anew in the sacrament except by the change of the substance of bread into Himself. However, when the change takes place, the thing that is converted does not remain and so, saving the truth of this sacrament, we can conclude that the substance of bread cannot remain after the consecration.”25 “There is no other way for Christ’s Body to begin to be in the sacrament except by the change of the substance of bread into it, a change that is rejected if we posit the annihilation of the bread or its resolution into preexisting matter.”26

This change is not like the cases of natural changes, but rather is only possible by God’s power: “Christ’s True Body is in this sacrament, and it does not begin to be there by local movement; nor is Christ’s Body there as in a place, as was said. So, it is necessary to say that Christ’s Body begins to be there on account of the change of the substance of bread into Himself. This change is not like natural changes, but is entirely supernatural, done only by God’s power. As Saint Ambrose says, in the book De Sacramentis, ‘It is obvious that the Virgin gave birth outside of the natural order; what we consecrate is the Body taken from the Virgin. Why, then, do you seek natural order in Christ’s Body, when the Lord Jesus Himself was born of the Virgin outside of the natural order?’ Commenting on John 6 [63], ‘the words I have spoken to you,’ namely, of this sacrament, ‘are spirit and life,’ Chrysostom says, ‘that is, they are spiritual, having nothing of carnal or natural consequence; rather, they are removed from all earthly necessities and the laws that are in place here.’”27

So, this is a work of God alone: “Every change made according to natural laws is formal. However, God is infinite act, as was said in the Prima Pars, and His action extends to the entire nature of being. So, not only can He bring about formal changes so that different forms succeed one after another in the same subject, but He can also bring about the total change of a being so that the entire substance of one is converted into the entire substance of another.

In this sacrament, this is done by the Divine Power, as the entire substance of bread is converted into the entire substance of Christ’s Body, and the entire substance of wine is converted into the entire substance of Christ’s Blood. Thus, this change is not formal, but rather substantial. Nor is this change contained among the species of natural changes; rather, it can be called with its proper name, ‘transubstantiation.’”28

It is a work of the Holy Spirit and of the words of consecration. In one of the objections, Saint Thomas posits: “Damascene says, in Book IV, ‘The change of bread into Christ’s Body is done only by the Holy Spirit’s power.’ The Holy Spirit’s power, however, is uncreated, and so by no created power of those words is the sacrament consecrated.”29 To this he responds: “Saying that the bread is converted into Christ’s Body only by the Holy Spirit’s power does not exclude the instrumental power which is in the form of the sacrament, just as when it is said that only the smith makes a knife, the power of the hammer is not excluded. ”30

We are not dealing with a natural or formal change, like the kinds that we know; in these changes, the form must be in the matter or in the subject, and here there is neither one nor the other: “This objection follows from formal change or conversion, as it is fitting, as was said, for the form to be in the matter or the subject. However, this does not take place in a complete substantial change, as there is no subject to receive them.”31 “Properly speaking, this change does not have a subject, as was said; however, the accidents that remain have some similitude to the subject.”32

This is the way it is for the simple reason that God is God and He is the author of being: “The power of a finite agent cannot change one form into another, nor one material into another. However, the power of an infinite agent can make such a change, because its action reaches all being, and the nature of being is common to all forms and all matter. The author of being can convert what there is of being into something different, removing that by which they were distinguished from each other.”33

This change is instantaneous for three reasons: first, because the substance of Christ’s Body, the end of the change in itself, does not admit of a “more” or “less” – that is, it impossible for the transubstantiation to be gradual; secondly, there is no subject to be successively prepared. Thirdly, this change is done by God’s infinite power.34

The bread becomes Christ’s Body, but Christ’s Body does not become bread: “The change of bread into Christ’s Body has some elements in common with creation and natural transmutation, but in others it differs. The order of the ends is common to the three, that is, one thing comes after another. In creation, being comes after non-being, as in this sacrament Christ’s Body comes after the substance of bread, and in natural transmutations white follows black, or fire follows air. Likewise, in all three these ends do not occur simultaneously.

The change that we are speaking about is like creation because in neither change is there a common subject at either extreme end of the change. The contrary, however, is true for all natural transmutations.

However, this change does have two things in common with natural transmutations, though not in the same way. First, [in both] one of the extremes passes into the other, as the bread into Christ’s Body, and air into fire; however, non-being is not converted into being. This [passing of the extremes], however, happens in different ways in both, as in this sacrament the entire substance of bread passes into the whole Body of Christ. In natural transmutations, however, the matter of one takes up the form of the other, leaving behind the form that it had. Secondly, they have this in common, that in both ends of the change something remains the same, which does not happen in creation. This, however, happens differently, for in natural transmutation the same matter or subject remains; in this sacrament, it is the accidents that remain the same.

From this, we can qualify the different ways in which we must speak about these matters, because in none of these three ways are the extremes present simultaneously, and so in no way can we predicate one extreme of another by using the substantive verb in the present tense. We do not say, therefore, ‘Non-being is being,’ or ‘Bread is Christ’s Body,’ or ‘Air is fire,’ or ‘White is black.’

However, on account of the order of the extremes in all of them, we can use the preposition ‘ex’ [meaning “out of” or “from”] which describes order. We can therefore truly and properly say that ‘being is made out of non-being,’ ‘from bread, Christ’s Body,’ ‘from air, fire,’ or ‘from white, black.’

However, because in creation one extreme does not pass into the other, we cannot use the word ‘change’ in creation, as if to say ‘non-being is changed into being.’ We can, though, use this word in this sacrament, just as we can for natural transmutation. However, because in this sacrament the whole substance is converted into another, on this account the change is properly called ‘transubstantiation.’

Again, as there is no subject of this change, things that are said of natural changes on account of the subject are not granted in this change. First, it is clear that the potency to be the opposite follows upon the subject, and for this reason we say that ‘what is white can be black,’ or that ‘air can be fire.’ The second statement is not as proper as the first, for the subject of whiteness, in which there is a potency to blackness, is the whole substance of that which is white, since whiteness is not a substantial part of it. The subject of the form of air is a part of the substance, and thus when it is said that ‘air can be fire,’ it is verified by synecdoche on account of the part.

In this change [of transubstantiation], though, and likewise in creation, since there is no subject, it cannot be said that one extreme can be the other, just as ‘non-being can be being,’ or ‘bread can be Christ’s Body.’ For the same reason, it cannot be properly said that ‘of [‘de’] non-being being is made’ or that ‘of [‘de’] bread Christ’s Body is made,’ because this preposition ‘de’ [meaning “of”] designates the consubstantiality or the same substance at the extremes. This does happen in the extremes of natural transmutations, because the two ends have the same subject. For the same reason, to say that ‘the bread will be Christ’s Body,’ or that ‘bread may become Christ’s Body’ is not permissible, just as it is not permissible to say that in creation ‘non-being will be being’ or ‘non-being may become being.’ This way of speaking is correct in natural transmutations by reason of the subject, as when we say that ‘what is white becomes black,’ or ‘a white thing will be black.’

Nevertheless, since in this sacrament something remains the same after the change, namely, the accidents of bread, as was said above, on account of the similitude some of these expressions can be permitted, for example, that ‘bread becomes Christ’s Body,’ or that ‘bread will be Christ’s Body,’ or that ‘from bread Christ’s Body is made.’ This can be done if the word ‘bread’ is understood not as the substance of bread, but rather in general, as ‘that which is contained under the species of bread,’ under which species were first contained the substance of bread, and afterwards Christ’s Body.”35 terminorum, scilicet ut post hoc sit hoc, in creatione enim est esse post non esse, in hoc sacramento corpus Christi post substantiam panis, in transmutatione naturali album post nigrum vel ignis post aerem; et quod praedicti termini non sint simul. Convenit autem conversio de qua nunc loquimur cum creatione, quia in neutra earum est aliquod commune subiectum utrique extremorum. Cuius contrarium apparet in omni transmutatione naturali. Convenit vero haec conversio cum transmutatione naturali in duobus, licet non similiter. Primo quidem, quia in utraque unum extremorum transit in aliud, sicut panis in corpus Christi, et aer in ignem, non autem non ens convertitur in ens. Aliter tamen hoc accidit utrobique. Nam in hoc sacramento tota substantia panis transit in totum corpus Christi, sed in transmutatione naturali materia unius suscipit formam alterius, priori forma deposita. Secundo conveniunt in hoc, quod utrobique remanet aliquid idem, quod non accidit in creatione. Differenter tamen, nam in transmutatione naturali remanet eadem materia vel subiectum; in hoc autem sacramento remanent eadem accidentia. Et ex his accipi potest qualiter differenter in talibus loqui debeamus. Quia enim in nullo praedictorum trium extrema sunt simul ideo in nullo eorum potest unum extremum de alio praedicari per verbum substantivum praesentis temporis, non enim dicimus, non ens est ens, vel, panis est corpus Christi, vel, aer est ignis aut album nigrum. Propter ordinem vero extremorum, possumus uti in omnibus hac praepositione ex, quae ordinem designat. Possumus enim vere et proprie dicere quod ex non ente fit ens, et ex pane corpus Christi, et ex aere ignis vel ex albo nigrum. Quia vero in creatione unum extremorum non transit in alterum, non possumus in creatione uti verbo conversionis, ut dicamus quod non ens convertitur in ens. Quo tamen

The change of the bread and the wine into the Savior’s Body and Blood is so admirable, singular, unique, and exceptional that it is much more difficult than the creation of the world: “In this change there are many things that are more difficult than creation, in which there is only one difficulty: making something out of nothing. This, however, pertains to the First Cause’s proper mode of production, which supposes nothing for its operation. However, transubstantiation is difficult not only in that this whole is converted into that whole, in such a way that nothing of the first might remain (which does not pertain to any cause’s common mode of production), but moreover it has this difficulty: the accidents remain while the substance is removed. There are many other difficulties that will be discussed later. Nevertheless, the word ‘change’ is acceptable in reference to this sacrament, though not, however, in reference to creation.”36

This is the work of the Creator’s active power: “As was said above, potency belongs to the subject, but there is no subject in this change. Thus, it cannot be granted that the bread can be Christ’s Body, and therefore this change does not happen on account of the creature’s passive potency, but rather only by the Creator’s active power.”37

It is a miraculous change: “In this sacrament the consecration of the matter consists in the miraculous change of the substance, which only God can do. Thus, in this sacrament the minister performing it has no action other than pronouncing the words.”38

The form of the consecration of the bread, “This is My Body,” is very fitting: “This is a fitting form for the consecration of the bread. It was said that this consecration consists in the change of the substance of bread into Christ’s Body. However, the sacrament’s form should signify what is done in the sacrament. Thus the form of the consecration should signify the very change of the bread into Christ’s Body. In this, three things are to be considered, namely, the change itself, the starting point or the end from which the change begins [terminus a quo], and the end to which the change tends and ultimately ends [terminus ad quem].

The change, in turn, can be considered in two ways: first, in its ‘becoming’ [fieri] and secondly in its being finished or done [in facto esse]. However, change should not be signified in this form as ‘becoming,’ but rather in the sense of being finished or done. This is, first, because such a change is not successive, as was said above, but rather instantaneous, and thus in such changes ‘becoming’ is nothing other than ‘being finished or done.’ Secondly, it is because the sacramental forms signify the effects of the sacraments as artificial forms signify the effects of art. An artificial form represents the ultimate or last effect to which the artist’s intention is directed. In this way, the artificial form in the mind of the one who builds is principally the form of the house constructed and, as a consequence, the construction. Thus, in this form the change should be expressed as ‘being finished or done,’ to which the intention is referred.

Since the change is expressed in this form as ‘being finished or done,’ it is necessary that the extremes of the change be signified as they are in the completed change. The end ‘to which’ has the nature of its own substance but the end ‘from which’ does not remain in its own substance, but only as to its accidents by which it is known by the senses and can be made out by them. Thus, it is fitting to express the end ‘from which’ by the demonstrative pronoun [“this”] referring to the sensible accidents which remain. However, the end ‘to which’ is expressed by the noun that signifies the nature of the thing which ends the change, which is Christ’s entire Body, and not only His flesh, as was already said. Thus, the most fitting form is ‘This is My Body.’”39

SACRAMENT AND SACRIFICE

“Reception belongs to the nature of sacrament; 40

oblation, to that of sacrifice.”

SAINT THOMAS

In this chapter, we’ll see how Saint Thomas understands the Eucharist as a sacrament and as a sacrifice. We’ll do this by reading and commenting on some texts from the Summa Theologica, in such a way that we’ll penetrate deeper and deeper into the topic and see it more and more clearly.

In the treatise on the Eucharist, the word “sacrifice” is used some fifty times.

We can organize the texts that I have selected into three groups, which will be the three points to develop:

1. What distinguishes the Eucharist as sacrament from the Eucharistic sacrifice?

2. In some texts we will see how the two elements mutually illuminate each other, because, in Saint Thomas’s mind, they are not airtight compartments, but rather it is the reality of the Eucharist that it is both a sacrament and a sacrifice;

3. Thirdly, and this is important to emphasize, in which moment, according to Saint Thomas, the sacrament is carried out and in which moment the sacrifice occurs.

1. What distinguishes them?

We begin with a text from the Summa Theologica where Saint Thomas makes a distinction that is essential for understanding what follows: “[The Eucharist] is simultaneously a sacrifice and a sacrament”–and immediately he gives the reason why it is both one thing and the other–“it has the nature of a sacrifice insofar as it is offered, and it has the nature of a sacrament insofar as it is received.”41 This is the crucial text for the entire treatise and for understanding that mysterious reality which is the Eucharist. The Eucharist is a sacrament, because what is essential to a sacrament is man’s sanctification, but also a sacrifice, because what is essential to a sacrifice is the glorification of God. As a sacrament, the Eucharist is a permanent reality; as a sacrifice, it is, as theologians say, an actio transeuns.

Later on, Saint Thomas will again insist on this point, recalling what he said above: “As was said earlier, this sacrament is not only a sacrament, but also a sacrifice.”42

In the reply to the first objection, where a comparison is made between the other sacraments, Saint Thomas very briefly replies that, with respect to the Eucharist: “This sacrament has something above all the rest, which is the fact that it is a sacrifice.”43 It is for this reason that it is more excellent than all the other sacraments.

A little further on, Saint Thomas deals with a very interesting question, and one very pertinent today, about whether or not the priest needs to receive Communion at Mass. He responds by citing the Council of Toledo’s authority as an argument. However, just as the body of the article begins, he again takes up the idea that we pointed out earlier: “I answer, as was said earlier, that the Eucharist is not only a sacrament, but also a sacrifice.”44 It is from this perspective that he will give the reasons why the priest should always receive Communion at Mass: “Whoever offers a sacrifice should be a sharer in the sacrifice because, as Augustine says, the exterior sacrifice that he offers is a sign of the inner sacrifice by which he offers himself to God. Thus, by this participation in the sacrifice, he shows that the inner sacrifice is also his. In like manner, by distributing the sacrifice to the people he shows that he is the dispenser of the Divine to the people. . . . Therefore he should receive it before dispensing it to the people. . . . ‘What kind of sacrifice is it if not even the one who sacrifices is recognized as a partaker of it?”45 For this reason, communion is an integral part of the sacrifice; it is not essential, as some say, but it is a truly integral part. The sacrifice cannot take place entirely if there is no communion; communion must take place so that the sign be complete: “However, it is by consuming the sacrifice that he becomes a participant in it, according to what the Apostle says ‘Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar?’ [1 Cor 10:18]. Therefore, it is necessary that each time the priest consecrates, he receive the sacrament in its entirety.”46

It is wonderful to see what Saint Thomas’s mind is like: his is truly remarkable. We discover this not only from examining the order in the questions that he treats, or in the order of the articles of each question. Rather, we see his genius as he goes about weaving a train of thought through different questions and articles, in the course of which he never contradicts himself. Indeed, he establishes a perfect harmony in all his teachings with respect to a very difficult topic like the Eucharistic mystery. Saint Bonaventure will say: “inter sacramenta, cetera est difficillimum ad credendum, immo inter credibilia” (“Among the sacraments, it is the most difficult to believe, indeed, even among all the other things that we must believe”).47

In the response to the first objection in the same article, when he confronts the topic in relation to the chrism (and thus to any other matter of the other sacraments) Saint

Thomas says: “The consecration of chrism or of any other matter is not a sacrifice as the consecration of the Eucharist is.”48

In the following question, Saint Thomas gives a sort of catechesis regarding the celebration of the Eucharist, and in the corpus of the article he will say the following: “As the people have been prepared and instructed [and after the preparation of the gifts in the offertory] the time approaches for the celebration of the mystery which is offered as a sacrifice and consecrated and consumed as a sacrament [and this he explains marvelously]: first is the completion of the oblation or offering, secondly the consecration of the matter offered, and thirdly, the consummation of said offering. Regarding the oblation, two things are done, namely, the people offer praise. . . . and the priest prays, asking that the people’s oblation be accepted by God. . . . Regarding the consecration, which is done by supernatural power, the people are first excited to devotion in the preface in which they are admonished to lift their hearts up to the Lord.”49 This is because only with hearts lifted up to God can that most excellent divine action, the sacrifice of the Cross, be understood. This is also what is expressed in the response to the fifth objection, where Saint Thomas cites Saint Cyprian: “In saying the preface, the priest disposes the minds of the brethren saying, ‘Lift up your hearts,’ and when the people answer ‘We lift them up to the Lord,’ let them remember that they are to think of nothing but God.”50

2. How the aspects illuminate each other

I have chosen two texts in order to show how the two aspects shed light on each other, that is, the aspect of sacrament on that of sacrifice, and that of sacrifice on sacrament. This is because the two aspects are indissolubly united.

Question 79, article 7 [Whether this sacrament benefits others besides the recipients?], the response to the third objection is really very beautiful: “Receiving belongs to the very notion of sacrament, but oblation pertains to the notion of sacrifice. Thus, when one or even several receive Christ’s Body, no help is given to others. Similarly, even when multiple hosts are consecrated by the priest at one Mass, the effects of this sacrament are not multiplied, because there is only one sacrifice. Nor is there any more power in several hosts than in one, since under all the hosts and under one host, the entire Christ is present. Thus, if anyone were to consume multiple consecrated hosts in one Mass, he would not receive any greater effect from the sacrament. However, the oblation of the sacrifice is multiplied in several Masses, and likewise the effect of the sacrifice and of the sacrament is multiplied.”51 This is a thought that can be developed even more; these are teachings that can serve as entire meditations.

Responding to the first objection of the first article of question 83, Saint Thomas cites Saint Ambrose in a text that we know very well: “Saint Ambrose says, ‘The victim is one,’ that is, the one which Christ offered and which we offer, ‘and not many, for Christ was offered once, and the former sacrifice is the model of the latter. Therefore, just as Christ’s Body is one, and not many bodies, no matter where it is offered, so too is the sacrifice but one.”52

Paul VI teaches: “Sacrifice and Sacrament pertain to the same mystery and cannot be separated from each other. The Lord is immolated in an unbloody way in the Sacrifice of the Mass and He re-presents the sacrifice of the Cross and applies its salvific power at the moment when he becomes sacramentally present—through the words of consecration—as the spiritual food of the faithful, under the appearances of bread and wine.”53

For this reason, the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches us: “The Mass is at the same time, and inseparably, the sacrificial memorial in which the sacrifice of the cross is perpetuated and the sacred banquet of communion with the Lord’s body and blood.”54

The Compendium sees this in the symbol of the altar: “The altar is the symbol of Christ himself who is present both as sacrificial victim (the altar of the sacrifice) and as food from heaven which is given to us (the table of the Lord).”55

3. Moments in which these aspects are carried out

The sacrificial oblation is carried out in the moment of the consecration of the Eucharist, as we have seen in the text just cited from Paul VI.

This the moment of the fullest expression of the verb ‘to be,’ the king of the verbs: “This is My Body. . . which will be given up. This is the chalice of My Blood. . . which will be shed. . . . This is the mystery of faith.” In that moment, “the word is added to the element, and there results the sacrament,”56 as Saint Augustine says. “The words . . . bring about only what they signify.”57

This is the moment of a gushing forth of verbs; there, in that very moment, a waterfall of verbs becomes present: to consecrate, to transubstantiate (the bread and the wine), to be able (on God’s part), to immolate (the Victim), to sacrifice, to make an oblation, to offer, to perpetuate (the memorial of the sacrifice of the Cross), to act (in Persona Christi), to make present, to actualize, to recall, to renew, to show, to prophesy, to give up, to shed, to propitiate, to impetrate, to represent, to remember, to apply, to consummate, to accept . . . the king of verbs takes us, as if by the hand, to the King of Words, to the One who is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev 19:16), to the Ipsum esse subsistens.58 Since it is the word of the Word Himself: “the Consecration is done with the Lord Jesus’ words and phrases. . . . Christ’s word makes the Sacrament.”59

That the Eucharist is a sacrifice also has pastoral consequences: “The opportunity of offering sacrifice is not considered only in relation to Christ’s faithful . . . but principally in relation to God to Whom the sacrifice is offered by consecration.”60 This is one of the questions discussed now-a-days: “If there are no people present, then the Eucharist shouldn’t be celebrated.” Fools! The Mass that is offered is offered to God, and the people benefit from it. If there are people present, then certainly the people present benefit more. However, even if there are no people there, they still benefit, because the Mass is offered for all people, and, for this reason, strictly speaking there is never a “Mass without people.” The people are always there, even though they might not be physically present. Moreover, the Mass that is offered to God has an infinite value, because it is always offered to God as a sacrifice. Those who have lost the value of Mass as a sacrifice do not celebrate it if there are no people, because (they say) it is only important when others are there; it is as though it were the people who gave the Mass its value! In reality, the Mass is principally important because of its relation to God, to whom the sacrifice is offered by consecration.

In a different section, the Angelic Doctor reminds us: “The other sacraments are confected when they are used by the faithful . . . . However, this Sacrament is confected in the Consecration of the Eucharist, in which the sacrifice is offered to God and which the priest is obligated to offer by the ordination that he has received.”61 He then cites that text from Scripture, from the Books of Maccabees (2 Macc 4:14), making reference to us priests and which can be applied to many today: “thus what is said in Second Maccabees, chapter four [v. 14], is said against some priests who ‘no longer cared about the service of the altar, disdaining the temple and neglecting the sacrifices.’”62

chapters.t: The eucharist and the other sacraments
chapters.h:
THE EUCHARIST AND THE OTHER SACRAMENTS

The Savior extolled 63

SAINT AUGUSTINE

Among the seven sacraments, we have one that is unique and that surpasses all the others in excellence for various reasons: this one is the Eucharist.

1. The Eucharist “contains truly, really, and substantially the Body and Blood, together with the soul and divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, and thus the entire Christ,” as the Council of Trent64 defined it and as the Catechism of the Catholic Church65 and the

Compendium66 remind us. The sacrament not only gives us grace, but also the Author of Grace Himself.

The other sacraments have a certain virtue (meaning power) given by Christ, but not Christ Himself. “In the other sacraments, Christ is not really present as He is in this sacrament. Thus, in the other sacraments the substance of matter remains, but not, however, in this sacrament,”67 in which, rather, the material is converted.

“Dionysius says ‘No one is granted a higher grade of perfection save by the most divine Eucharist.’ Thus, this sacrament is most powerful and perfects all the others. . . . Absolutely speaking, the sacrament of the Eucharist is the foremost among all the other sacraments, and this is for three reasons: first, from the fact that it contains Christ Himself substantially, whereas the other sacraments contain only a certain instrumental power which is a share (a participation) of Christ’s power, as was said above. What is by essence, however, is always superior to what is by participation. ”68

2. The Eucharist brings life to all the other sacraments. It is “almost the consummation of the spiritual life and the end of all of the sacraments, as all the sanctification produced by the other sacraments is as a preparation for receiving or consecrating the Eucharist.” 69 For this reason, “this sacrament, which contains Christ Himself, as Dionysius says, is perfective of all the others which participate in Christ’s virtue [power].”70

“This is made clear from the relation of the sacraments to each other, as in this way, all the other sacraments are seen as ordered to the Eucharist as their end. It is clear that the sacrament of Holy Orders is ordered to the consecration of the Eucharist, and the sacrament of Baptism to the reception of the Eucharist. Man is then perfected by Confirmation, so that he might not abstain from receiving this sacrament because of fear. Both Reconciliation and Extreme Unction [Last Rites or Anointing of the Sick] prepare man to receive Christ’s Body worthily. At least in its meaning, Marriage touches this sacrament insofar as it signifies the union of Christ with the Church, the unity of which the Eucharist is a figure. Thus the Apostle says ‘This is a great mystery, but I speak in reference to Christ and the church’ [Eph 5:32]. Lastly, this [how all the sacraments are ordered to the Eucharist] is apparent from the rites of the sacraments, as almost all of the sacraments end in the Eucharist . . . as is evident from the cases of those who are ordained and then receive Communion, and also those baptized, if they are adults.”71 “Marriage is ordered to the common corporeal good; however, the spiritual common good of the entire Church is itself substantially contained in the sacrament of the Eucharist.”72

3. In addition to being a sacrament, the Eucharist is also a sacrifice:

This is not the case for the other sacraments. “The consecration of chrism or of any other matter is not a sacrifice as the consecration of the Eucharist is.”73

“Above all the other sacraments, this sacrament is also a sacrifice.”74

4. The matter of the sacrament, bread and wine, are consecrated: “this sacrament is confected by the consecration of the matter, while all the other sacraments are confected in the use of consecrated matter.”75

The matter, such as water, oil, and so on, is not consecrated in the other sacraments: “the consecration of the matter in the other sacraments consists only in a blessing from which the consecrated matter instrumentally receives some spiritual power which can come through the priest, the animated [living] instrument, to inanimate [non-living] instruments. However, in the Eucharist the consecration of the matter consists in a miraculous change of substance which only God can bring about. Thus, in confecting this sacrament, the minister has no act other than to say the words.”76

5. As a consequence, the Eucharist and the other sacraments also differ in the form of the words of the rite: “As the form should be fitting to the thing, the form of this sacrament differs from the forms of the other sacraments in two respects. The first respect is insofar as the form of the other sacraments implies the use of matter, as, for instance, in Baptism and Confirmation. However, the form of this sacrament only implies the consecration of the matter which consists in transubstantiation, as it is said, ‘This is My Body,’ or ‘This is the chalice of My Blood.’ The second respect is insofar as the forms of the other sacraments are pronounced in the person of the minister, either by way of exercising an act, as when it is said, ‘I baptize you,’ or ‘I confirm you,’ etc., by way of a command, as it is said in Holy Orders, ‘Receive the power,’ etc., or by way of supplication, as in the sacrament of Extreme Unction it is said, ‘By this anointing and our intercession,’ etc. However, the form of this sacrament of the Eucharist is pronounced as if Christ Himself were speaking in person, so that it is to be understood that the minister does nothing in perfecting this sacrament other than to pronounce Christ’s words.”77

6. The matter, and thus the consecration, is two-fold: bread and wine. We have already cited some texts regarding this (point 4), but let us add some others: “This sacrament is perfected or brought about in the consecration of the matter. . . . However, in this sacrament the matter is two-fold.” The body of the article, however, clarifies: “Corporeal refreshment requires two things, namely food, which is dry nourishment, and drink, which is wet nourishment. Consequently, two things come together for the integrity of this sacrament: spiritual food and spiritual drink, according to what John 6 [56] says, ‘My Flesh is true food, and My Blood is true drink.’ Therefore, this sacrament is multiple in the material sense, but one formally and perfectively.”78

In the Eucharist, both the matter and the consecration are two-fold in order to adequately represent the Passion: “Our Lord’s Passion is represented in the very consecration of this sacrament, and so the Body should not be consecrated without the Blood.”79

In the other sacraments, however, the matter is only one: “Water is the proper matter of Baptism.” “Chrism is the fitting matter of this sacrament [of Confirmation].” “In Penance, whose quasi-matter are the three acts of the penitent that, as is said, constitute the three parts of said sacrament (a contrite heart, oral confession, and satisfaction for sins). . . .” “In Extreme Unction, whose matter is olive oil blessed by the bishop. . . .”80

There is also only one blessing or consecration of the matter of the other sacraments, both because of the use Christ Himself made of the matter as well as on account of the minister’s action: “All of the sanctifying power of the sacraments is derived from Christ Himself. . . . It should noticed, however, that Christ did use certain sacraments having a corporeal [determined] matter, as in Baptism and the Eucharist. Thus, from the very use that Christ made of them, the matter of these sacraments received an aptitude for the perfection of the sacrament. Thus, the Lord Himself ‘taking bread, blessed it,’ and in a like manner, the chalice, as

Saint Matthew [26:26-27] and Saint Luke [22:19-20] have said. For this reason, it is not necessary for [the confection of] these sacraments that the matter be blessed previously, because Christ’s blessing is sufficient. If any blessing be used, it belongs to the solemnity of the sacrament, and not as something necessary. However, Christ did not make use of visible anointings, so as not to insult or diminish the invisible anointing with which He was ‘anointed above His fellows’ [cfr. Ps 45:8]. Thus, both the chrism and the holy oil [Oil of the Sick] are blessed prior to being put to sacramental use. . . .” “Corporeal matter is not capable of receiving grace as if it were the subject of it, but only as it is an instrument of grace. . . . Thus the matter of this sacrament is consecrated, either by Christ Himself or by the bishop, who represents the person of Christ in the Church.”81

7. In fieri et in facto esse.

The only sacrament that has these two moments, in fieri and in facto esse, is the Eucharist: 1. In fieri, meaning, in the becoming or bringing about, the constitutive moment of the consecration, and 2. In facto esse, meaning in its being finished or done, in its permanence or remaining, that is, until communion or until it is reserved in the tabernacle; this is because, unlike all the other sacraments,82 the Eucharist is not confected in the moment of its administration. Rather, it is confected first and given or administered later. “This consecration consists in the change of the substance of bread into Christ’s Body. However, the sacrament’s form should signify what is done in the sacrament. Thus the form of the consecration should signify the very change of the bread into Christ’s Body. In this, three things are to be considered, namely, [1] the change itself, [2] the starting point or the ‘end from which’ [terminus a quo], and [3] the ending point or the ‘end to which’ [terminus ad quem].

[1] The change, in turn, can be considered in two ways: first, in its ‘becoming’ [in fieri] and secondly in its ‘being finished or done’ [in facto esse]. However, in the form of consecration change should not be signified as a ‘becoming,’ but rather in the sense of ‘being finished or done.’ This is, first, because such a change is not successive . . . but rather instantaneous, and thus in such changes ‘becoming’ is nothing other than ‘being finished or done.’ Secondly, it is because the sacramental forms signify the effects of the sacraments as artificial forms signify the effects of art. . . . Thus, in this form the change should be expressed as in ‘being finished or done,’ to which the intention is referred.

[2 and 3] Since the change is expressed in this form as ‘being finished or done,’ it is necessary that both ends of the change be signified as they are in the completed change. However, the end ‘to which’ has the nature of its own substance but the end ‘from which’ does not remain in its own substance, but only as to its accidents by which it is known by the senses and can be made out by them. Thus, it is fitting to express the end ‘from which’ by the demonstrative pronoun [‘this’] referring to the sensible accidents which remain. However, the end ‘to which’ is expressed by the noun that signifies the nature of the thing which ends the change, which is Christ’s entire Body, and not only His flesh, as was already said. Thus, the most fitting form is ‘This is My Body.’”83

8. In addition to being signs, the sacraments of the New Law are causes that produce what they signify.

a) The other sacraments work through a divine power that is in them and that makes them instruments of the Holy Spirit, as happens with the water in Baptism.

However, in the Eucharist the accidents of the consecrated bread and wine sanctify those who receive them, although that supernatural power is not connected immediately with the power that comes from heaven, but rather mediately through the Lord’s Body and Blood which are contained in them: “The water of Baptism does not cause any spiritual effect because it is water, but rather because of the Holy Spirit’s power that is in the water. For this reason Chrysostom says, commenting on the Gospel of Saint John [5:4] ‘For from time to time an angel of the Lord used to come down into the pool; and the water was stirred up, etc.’: ‘The water alone does not act upon the baptized, but rather, when it receives the grace of the Holy Spirit, it then loosens all sins.’ The relation of Holy Spirit’s power to the water of Baptism is the same as the relation of Christ’s true Body to the species of bread and wine. Thus, the species of bread and wine have no effect except from the power of Christ’s true Body.”84 b) Likewise, the other sacraments differ from the Eucharist in how they produce the two effects that are called res et sacramentum and res tantum. Res tantum indicates that which is only an effect. Res et sacramentum is that which, in addition to being an effect of the sacramentum tantum, is also an active cause of all the effects that follow. In the Eucharist, what is simply the effect, res tantum, is the sacramental grace given to us when we receive Communion: sanctifying and cibative85 grace, union with Christ and with our brothers and sisters, union with the Church, charity, peace, and so on; the res et sacramentum is the Lord’s Body and Blood, under the Eucharistic species.

There are sacraments that give these two effects immediately; this is the case, for example, in baptism, which gives the character (that is, the indelible, unrepeatable, and causal supernatural power) and the grace of spiritual birth.

In contrast, the Eucharist doesn’t give both effects immediately. In its ‘becoming’ [in fieri] Christ’s words and the Holy Spirit’s power carry out the Transubstantiation that places Christ’s Body and Blood sacramentally under the Eucharistic species; in its ‘being finished or done’ [in facto esse], the consecrated species make the sacramental presence, brought about in the first moment, to remain under those species. While the species remain, Christ’s Body and Blood remain as well; when the species disappear, so will the Body and Blood.

c) The other sacraments are brought about in their being administered, and everything produced by these sacraments is in the one who receives them; for example, in Baptism the res et sacramentum, the sacramental character, and the res tantum, grace, are both produced when Baptism is administered and are produced in the person who is baptized.

In the Eucharist, under the aspect of in fieri as well as in facto esse, the Body and Blood are outside of the one who will receive communion; the first and second sacramental effects are produced right when the person receives communion.

This is why Saint Thomas teaches what he does: “A sacrament is called such because it contains something sacred. Something can be sacred in two ways: in absolute, or by relation to another thing. This is precisely the difference that there is between the Eucharist and the other sacraments that have sensible material: while the Eucharist contains something sacred absolutely, namely, Christ Himself, the water of Baptism, however, contains something sacred by its relation to something else, that is, the power to sanctify. The same happens with the chrism and the other sacraments. From here it follows that the Eucharist is confected in the very consecration of the matter, while the other sacraments are confected in the use of consecrated matter.

From here follows another difference: in the Eucharist, the ‘res et sacramentum’ is in the matter itself; what is ‘res tantum,’ that is, the grace conferred, is only in the one who receives it. In baptism, both things are in the one who receives the sacrament, namely, the character which is the ‘res et sacramentum,’ and the grace of the remission of sins, which is the ‘res tantum.’ The same happens in all the other sacraments.”86

Accordingly, in the mystery of the Eucharist we can see:

That it is “the sacrament of the Church’s unity”87 That it is not simply a sacrament, but rather the sacrament par excellence: “Christ’s Passion is the origin of all sacraments, because, as the saints say, when He was hanging on the cross, it was from His open side that the sacraments flowed. The perfection of the sacraments is in the fact that they contain grace. The end of the sacraments, however, is two-fold: the proximate end, which is the sanctification of the one who receives it, and the ultimate or last end, which is eternal life. All of these aspects are found with a certain excellence in the Eucharist.”88 “First, because this sacrament is especially in memory of the Lord’s Passion, which is why it says ‘Do this in remembrance of me’; thus, with respect to its origin, it is called a sacrifice or host. In a similar way, the Eucharist doesn’t contain grace in an intentional way, as the other sacraments do; rather, it contains the very fullness of grace in the source itself. This is why it is called ‘Eucharist’ [‘good grace’] antonomastically.”89 “Thus the answer to the objections is made clear: from what is common to many, something can be named antonomastically or par excellence.”90 “‘The mystery of faith’ can refer to the Passion itself, which is a mystery of faith in as much as it is something that lies hidden in the faith of all the Christian faithful, and even more so for the ancients, for whom the mystery was concealed in different figures. It also refers to the Lord’s very Blood, in as much as it is contained in the sacrament, hidden under the species, and is very difficult to believe. For this reason, the Eucharist is called ‘the mystery of faith’ antonomastically.”91 “To the first objection, I reply that this sacrament cannot be confected without bread made from wheat. This is because of Divine institution, since Christ Himself confected it with this bread. We can give three reasons for this institution. The first comes from the effects: this bread gives the best nourishment, and so it is fitting for signifying the excellence of the grace that this sacrament confers.”92 “What is common to all the sacraments is antonomastically attributed to the Eucharist on account of its excellence.”93 “There is no better sacrament than the Eucharist”94 “This sacrament is of greatest worth among them all.”95 “The devotion required by this sacrament is greater than in all the other sacraments, because the entirety of Christ is contained within it. It also requires a more widespread devotion, as it requires the devotion of all people, since this sacrifice is offered for them, and not only for those who receive it, which is the case in the other sacraments.”96 “The Eucharist is called the sacrament of charity.”97 “This sacrament is the greatest sacrament.”98 “This is the sacrament of piety.”99 “This sacrament . . . deserves the greatest reverence.”100 Referring to Christ lifting up His eyes: “He had even more reason to do so in the institution of this sacrament, as it is something of greatest importance.”101 “such great mysteries”102 “This sacrament contains the entire mystery of our salvation, and so it is carried out with greater solemnity than the other sacraments.”103

For these, and for many other reasons, the Second Vatican Council teaches that the Eucharist is:

“the fount and apex of the whole Christian life”104 and that “the other sacraments, as well as with every ministry of the Church and every work of the apostolate, are tied together with the Eucharist and are directed toward it [S. Th., III, q. 73, a. 3, corpus; III, q. 65, a. 3]. The Most Blessed Eucharist contains the entire spiritual boon of the Church, [cfr. S. Th., III, q. 65, a. 3, ad 1; III, q. 79, a. 1, corpus and ad 1], that is, Christ Himself, our Pasch and Living Bread, by the action of the Holy Spirit through His very flesh vital and vitalizing, giving life to men who are thus invited and encouraged to offer themselves, their labors and all created things, together with Him.

In this light, the Eucharist shows itself as the source and the apex of the whole work of preaching the Gospel. Those under instruction are introduced by stages to a sharing in the Eucharist, and the faithful, already marked with the seal of Baptism and Confirmation, are through the reception of the Eucharist fully joined to the Body of Christ.”105

FOOD AND DRINK (CIBUS – POTUS)

“We leave that table like fire-breathing lions, 106

made into terrors for the devil”

SAINT JOHN CHRYSOSTOM

These two words appear together in reference to the Eucharist some seventeen times in the Summa. Saint Thomas begins his treatise by making a comparison between the life of the body and the spiritual life as follows: “The Church’s sacraments are ordered to helping man in his spiritual life. Now, the spiritual life is analogous to the life of the body, because corporeal things have a similitude to spiritual things. It is clear that for bodily life, man needs generation or birth in order to begin that life; he also needs to grow, in order to reach fullness or perfection of life, and this growth in turn requires food, so that he can maintain his life. It is like this for the spiritual life: it was fitting that there be baptism, which is spiritual generation or birth, Confirmation, which is spiritual growth, and the sacrament of the Eucharist, which is spiritual food. ”107

The Eucharist “is ordered to spiritual refreshment, which is similar to bodily refreshment. Two things are required for bodily refreshment: food, which is dry [solid] sustenance, and drink, which is wet [liquid] sustenance. These two fit together for the sacrament’s integrity and completeness, so that there is spiritual food and spiritual drink, as is said in the Gospel according to John ‘For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.’ So, this sacrament is many in the material sense, but formally and perfectively it is only one.”108

The two species, bread and wine, explicitly point out that the Eucharist is meant to be consumed as sustenance: “Christ instituted this sacrament under the species of bread and wine, as the Gospel according to Matthew says. Accordingly, bread and wine are the fitting matter for this sacrament. This is reasonable as we can see, first, in the use of this sacrament: it is used by eating it. Just as water is used in baptism for spiritual cleansing because water is commonly used to cleanse the body, so too, are bread and wine, which are commonly eaten, used in this sacrament for spiritual eating.”109 However, these species also show that the Eucharist is a sacrifice: “This is seen, secondly, in relation to Christ’s Passion, in which the blood was separated from the body. Thus, in this sacrament, which is the memorial of the Lord’s Passion, the bread, as the sacrament of the body, is received separately from the wine, as the sacrament of the blood.” The species also show us the effects that the Eucharist produces in man by caring for his body and his soul: “Thirdly, we see this in the effect, considered in each person who partakes of it. As Saint Ambrose says, ‘This sacrament works for the defense of body and soul’; it is for this reason that ‘Christ’s Body is offered (under the species of bread) for the body’s health, but His Blood (under the species of wine) for the soul’s health,’ as Leviticus 17 [14] says, ‘the life of all flesh is in the blood.’” Moreover, the species also point towards union with Christ and union amongst ourselves, that is, the unity of the Church: “Fourthly, we see this with respect to the effect on the whole Church, which is made up of many faithful, ‘just as bread is made from many grains, and wine flows from many grapes,’ as the gloss says on 1 Cor 10:17: ‘We, though many, are one body.’ ”110

The Eucharist signifies and causes the Church’s unity: “As Augustine says when explaining John’s words, ‘this food and drink,’ that is, His Body and His Blood: ‘Christ wants us to understand this as the communion of His body and members, which is the Church in the predestined, called, justified, in His glorified saints, and in believers.’” 111 “The priest offers this [prayer] for Christ’s mystical body which is signified in this sacrament.” 112 “Christ’s mystical body is signified in this sacrament.”113

Christ’s Body and Blood are truly in this sacrament, in order to truly be food and drink: “Saint Hilary says, ‘As to the verity of the flesh and blood there is no room left for doubt. For now both from the declaration of the Lord Himself and our own faith, it is verily flesh and verily blood.’ Saint Ambrose says, ‘As the Lord Jesus Christ is truly God’s Son, so too is it Christ’s true Flesh that we consume, and His true Blood that we drink.’

That Christ’s Body and Blood are truly present in this sacrament can be detected neither by the senses nor by the understanding, but rather only by faith, which rests on divine authority. For this reason, regarding those words of Saint Luke, ‘This is my body, which will be given for you,’ Saint Cyril says, ‘Do not doubt as to whether or not this is true; rather, take the Savior’s words with faith for, since He is the truth, He does not lie.’

That Christ’s Body and Blood be truly present is fitting, first of all, for the perfection of the New Law. The sacrifices of the Old Law contained the true sacrifice of Christ’s Passion only in figure, according to what the Letter to the Hebrews says, ‘Since the law has only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very image of them.’ Therefore it was necessary that the sacrifice of the New Law, which was instituted by Christ, should have something more; it should certainly contain Christ Himself who has suffered [ipsum passum], and not only in meaning or in figure, but rather in the full reality of truth. Accordingly, this sacrament, which really contains Christ Himself, is, as Dionysius says in his Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, ‘perfective of all the other sacraments,’ in which Christ’s power is participated.

Secondly, this presence is also in accord with Christ’s charity; it was on account of His charity that He assumed a true body of our nature for our salvation. As what is most characteristic of friendship is, as the Philosopher says, ‘living together,’ He promises us His bodily presence as a reward, as we read in Matthew: ‘Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather.’ In the meantime, He does not deprive us of His bodily presence in this our pilgrimage, but rather unites us to Himself in this sacrament through the truth of His Body and His Blood. This is why He says, ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him.’ This is also why this sacrament is the sign of the greatest charity, and uplifts our hopes, for in it an intimate union between Christ and us takes place.

Thirdly, this presence is also fitting for the perfection of faith, which concerns not only Christ’s divinity, but also His humanity, according to what the Gospel of John says, ‘You have faith in God; have faith also in me.’ As faith is of things unseen, just as Christ invisibly shows us

His divinity, so too does He invisibly show us His flesh in this sacrament.”114

In response to the question, “Why do the accidents remain?,” Saint Thomas replies: “As Saint Augustine says . . . ‘Under the species of bread and wine which we see, we honor the Body and Blood which we do not see.’”115

Nunc et ipsius Domini professione, et fide nostra, Caro eius vere est cibus et Sanguis eius vere est potus.’ Et Ambrosius dicit . . . ‘sicut verus est Dei Filius Dominus Iesus Christus, ita vera Christi Caro est quam accipimus, et verus Sanguis eius est potus’”; “Verum Corpus Christi et Sanguinem esse in hoc sacramento, non sensu deprehendi potest, sed sola fide, quae auctoritati divinae innititur. Unde super illud Luc. XXII, [19] ‘hoc est Corpus meum quod pro vobis tradetur,’ dicit Cyrillus [In Luc., super XII,19: PG 72,92], ‘non dubites an hoc verum sit, sed potius suscipe verba Salvatoris in fide, cum enim sit veritas, non mentitur.’ Hoc autem conveniens est, primo quidem, perfectioni Novae Legis. Sacrificia enim Veteris Legis illud verum sacrificium passionis Christi continebant solum in figura, secundum illud Heb. X, [1] ‘umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam rerum imaginem.’ Et ideo oportuit ut aliquid plus haberet sacrificium

Saint Thomas gives his arguments starting from the conditions of the accidents as food and drink: “From our senses, it is evident that once the consecration is carried out, the accidents of bread and wine remain, which is reasonably done by Divine Providence.

First, it is not usual, but rather horrible, for men to eat human flesh and drink human blood. So, Christ’s flesh and blood are rather given to us to eat under species which are used more often by men, namely, bread and wine.

Secondly, the accidents remain so that the sacrament might not be mocked or made fun of by unbelievers, which would happen if we were to eat our Lord under His own and proper species.

Thirdly, when we consume our Lord’s Body and Blood invisibly, this increases the merits of our faith.”116

Why is it that under the appearance of bread the Lord’s entire Body is present, and not just the flesh? “It is by the sacrament’s power that contained under it, that is, under the species of bread, is not only Christ’s flesh, but rather Christ’s entire body, that is, bones, nerves, and so on. This is clear from the form of the sacrament, which does not say ‘This is My flesh,’ but rather, ‘This is My Body.’ Accordingly, when the Lord said [John 6:55] ‘My flesh is true food,’ flesh means the entire Body, because, according to human custom, flesh is seen as more appropriate for eating: men usually eat the flesh of animals and not their bones, nerves, or the like. ”117

If the entire Christ is contained under two species, it would seem that one of them is superfluous, since one would contain the other. Aquinas’s entire response is worth noting: “It must certainly be believed that the whole Christ is present under each sacramental species, and yet in a different way in each. Under the species of bread, Christ’s Body is present by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti], whereas the Blood is present by real concomitance, as was said of Christ’s soul and divinity. However, under the species of wine, Christ’s Blood is present by the sacrament’s power, whereas the Body is present by real concomitance, as are His soul and divinity. This is because now Christ’s Blood is not separated from His Body, unlike how it was at the time of His Passion and death. Thus, if someone had celebrated this sacrament then [at the time of Christ’s death], then Christ’s Body would have been present under the species of bread, but without the Blood, and under the species of wine would have been the Blood without the Body, because that is the way it was in reality. ”118

For this reason, “although the whole Christ is present under both species, this is not in vain.

First, this is because it represents His Passion, in which the Blood was separated from the Body; this is why the form for the consecration of the Blood makes mention of its shedding.

Secondly, it is fitting for the use of this sacrament that Christ’s Body be shown to the faithful as food, and His Blood as drink.

Thirdly, it is fitting because, as we have already said, ‘Christ’s Body is offered for the body’s health, but His Blood for the soul’s health.”119

If the matter of one of the two species is lacking (i.e., there is no bread to be found or wine that can be used), then the one species should not be consecrated without the other, “because this would not be a perfect or complete sacrifice.”120 It would seem, then, that the same should be said of receiving communion only under one species, as Aquinas affirms in one of the objections: “Furthermore, the eating of the body and the drinking of the blood must both happen for the perfection of this sacrament, as was said earlier. Therefore, if the body is consumed without the blood, the sacrament will be imperfect and incomplete. This seems to be sacrilege, as Pope Gelasius adds, ‘The division of one same mystery cannot come about without a great sacrilege.’ ”121 However, the reply makes a distinction: “The perfection of this sacrament does not consist in its use by the faithful, but rather in the consecration of the matter. Therefore, nothing is taken away from this sacrament’s perfection if the faithful receive only the Body without receiving the Blood, provided that the consecrating priest receives both.”122 In the reply that follows, we read: “The Lord’s passion is represented in the very consecration of this sacrament, and thus the Body should not be consecrated without the Blood. The faithful, however, can receive the Body without the Blood, and this does not cause any detriment to the sacrament; this is because the priest offers and receives the Blood on behalf of everyone, and because, as was said above, Christ is fully contained under either species.”123

If we take the word “flesh” to mean all of the other parts of the Body, such as bones, nerves, and so on, and we recall that blood is also a part of the human body, it would seem that the Blood should not be consecrated separately, just as none of the other parts are consecrated separately. To this Saint Thomas responds: “In Christ’s passion, of which this sacrament is the memorial, the other parts of the Body were not separated from each other as the Blood was; rather, the Body remained entire, as we read: ‘You shall not break any of its bones’ [Ex 12:46]. This is why the Blood is consecrated separately from the Body in this sacrament, but no other part is consecrated separately from the others.”124

Examining the figure of the Passover Lamb, it would seem that a person should only receive communion once a year; however, the manna from heaven, which was eaten every day, is also a figure of the Eucharist: “The reality should correspond to the figure. The Paschal Lamb, however, which was the principal figure of this sacrament, as was said above, was eaten only once a year, and only once a year does the Church celebrate Christ’s passion, of which this sacrament is the memorial. So, it seems that it is not permissible to receive this sacrament every day, but rather only once a year.”125 The reply that follows reads: “The Paschal Lamb was the figure of this sacrament mainly with respect to Christ’s Passion, which is represented by this sacrament. Hence, it was eaten only once a year, because ‘Christ suffered for sins once’ [1 Pet 3:18]. For this reason, the Church celebrates the memory of Christ’s passion once a year. However, in this sacrament, the memorial of Christ’s passion is given to us by way of food, which is eaten daily. In this respect, it is better represented by manna, which was given to the people every day in the desert.”126

It would also seem that Christ took and gave His disciples His impassible Body: “A gloss on Matthew’s words in chapter 17, ‘And he was transfigured before them,’ says, ‘At the supper, He gave to the disciples the body that He had by nature, neither mortal nor passible.’ On Leviticus 2:5, ‘If your offering . . . is fried on a griddle,’ a gloss reads, ‘The Cross, mightier than anything else, made Christ’s flesh suitable for eating, flesh that did not seem suitable before the Passion.’ However, Christ gave His body as something suitable to be eaten, and therefore he gave it just as it was after the Passion, namely, impassible and immortal.”127 To this, the Angelic Doctor replies: “It is said that Christ did not give His mortal and passible body at the supper because He didn’t give it in the mortal and passible manner [He gave it in the sacramental fashion]. The Cross made Christ’s flesh suitable for eating insofar as this sacrament represents Christ’s Passion.”128

For this reason: “It is appropriate that both, meaning, Body and Blood, be received, because the sacrament’s perfection lies in both. Therefore, because it pertains to the priest to consecrate and complete this sacrament, in no way should he receive Christ’s Body without receiving the Blood as well. ”129
