chapters.t: The different states of christ’s body in the eucharist
chapters.h:
THE DIFFERENT STATES OF CHRIST’S BODY IN THE EUCHARIST

“This sacrament is the sign of the greatest charity, and uplifts our

hopes, for in it an intimate union between Christ and us takes 130

place.”

SAINT THOMAS

We must now consider the different states that Christ had or could have had in the Eucharist. Without hesitation, we must affirm that the Consecration, the Eucharistic immolation, the memorial, what this sacrament brings about by its very nature, is to take and bring Christ’s Body and Blood just as they are found, in whatever state they are found, in such a way that the sacramental sacrifice does not produce some new state in Christ.

The sacrament itself does not give a new state to the Divine Person or to His Body and Body.131 The new states that Christ’s Body and Blood can have don’t come because of the sacrament (ex vi sacramenti, meaning because of the sacrament or by the sacrament’s power, ex vi verborum, meaning because of the words of consecration or by the power of the words, ex vi convertionis, meaning on account of or by the power of transubstantiation): “In virtue of the words we have in the Eucharist all those things, and only those things, which are contained in the formulas of consecration. . . . Let us give literal meaning to their every word, and we have the exact statement of what there is on the altar.”132 “Since the change of the bread and the wine does not end in the divinity or in Christ’s soul, it follows that Christ’s soul and divinity are not in this sacrament by the sacrament’s power, but rather on account of real concomitance. As the divinity never laid aside the assumed Body, wherever Christ’s Body is, His divinity must necessarily be there as well. Hence, His divinity must necessarily accompany His Body in this sacrament”133 (it’s obvious that bread and wine cannot be changed into Christ’s divinity or soul).134 These new states come to the Body and Blood . . . by natural concomitance (ex vi realis concomitantiae)! This theological reality is part of the dogmas of the Council of Trent;135 these words aren’t mere theological wordplay, but rather the statement of the truth found in the Eucharistic reality itself, a truth that lends all of its strength to supporting the fact that the Eucharist is a sacrifice.

As understood here, taken from its Latin roots, concomitance means (by a certain redundancy of the noun and adverb) the action of walking or joining together with another as a companion. Its Latin roots are cum (with) and comes (companion). What this means, then, is that Christ’s Body and Blood aren’t alone; they come accompanied. They are “escorted by friends . . . a cortège of splendours,”136 whom they never appear without. These friends are: divinity, dimensive quantity like the Body’s substance and other accidents, 137 the soul (which could, in theory, not be present), the mortal and passible or immortal and glorious state, and so on.

In order to understand this truth better, let’s consider the Mass at the different states of Jesus’ life: at the Last Supper, in the hypothetical case that it was celebrated at His death, and after His Resurrection.

1. At the Last Supper

Let’s imagine the Last Supper. At the most important and pivotal moment, Jesus institutes the Eucharist. He distributes it to the Apostles: “It is clear that the same Body that the Apostles saw in its own species [in propria specie] was received by them under the sacramental species [in specie sacramenti],”138 the very One who was seated at the head of the table. What happened is that what was passible was, in an impassible way, under the sacramental species, just as what was invisibly there was also present, in itself, visibly. This is why in the argument from authority Saint Thomas cited our friend Innocent III: “He gave His Body to His disciples just as He had it then.”139

In the third objection Saint Thomas poses the following difficulty: “The sacramental words spoken by the priest in the person of Christ [in persona Christi] are not more powerful than when they were offered by Christ Himself. Now, however, by the power of those sacramental words, Christ’s impassible and immortal Body is consecrated upon the altar. How much more would this have been true then.”140 Saint Thomas replies as follows: “The accidents of Christ’s Body are in this sacrament by real concomitance, and not by the sacrament’s power, for by this power only the substance of Christ’s Body [and Blood] come to be there. Thus, the power of the sacramental words extends to making Christ’s Body present, whatever might be the accidents that really exist in it.”141 The Abbot Vonier says that this “final phrase is a real stroke of genius.”142 “It is through the distinction between the virtue [power] of the sacrament and concomitance that we are able to preserve the sacrificial aspect of the Eucharist.”143

It’s been many years since I began to study the Eucharist. I was moved by a sort of intuition that only recently I’ve been able to put into words. The intuition that I had was that the reason why the Mass is a sacrifice must be very simple, just as all of God’s other great works are simple, since He is infinite Simplicity. I think that the traces of this are found in that last phrase of Saint Thomas: “Thus, the power of the sacramental words extends to making Christ’s Body [and Blood] present, whatever might be the accidents that really exist in it,” as, for example, in the different states of Christ’s existence. By reason of the words (and the sacramental signs), Christ’s Blood, on one hand, and His Body, on the other, are signified separately. Therefore, nothing else is needed. The double consecration leaves, on one hand, the substance of Christ’s Blood under the species of wine and, on the other, the substance of Christ’s Body under the appearance of bread; we need nothing more in order to have a sacramental sacrifice. This is where we have the mactatio mystica, the unbloody immolation.

At the Last Supper, in the Eucharistic Sacrament, Christ’s Blood was under the species of wine and His Body under the species of bread because of the words He spoke. As a result of concomitance, Christ’s Blood was also under the species of bread, and His Body under the species of wine; for the same reason, His Divinity, His soul, and the mortal and passible state of His human nature along with its accidents, were also found there.

This is because what is proper to this sacrament is to take and bring Christ’s Body and Blood just as they are found, in whatever state they are found.

2. In Death

Let’s now consider a hypothetical case. Let’s imagine that some Apostle was celebrating Mass or that the Eucharist, the Lord’s Body, was reserved in a tabernacle: a) at the moment in which Christ was left without any blood in His Body, completely bloodless, and b) at the moment when He died on the Cross, that is, when His soul separated from His Body. What would’ve happened in these cases?

a) When the Body was left without the Blood: “By the power of consecration, Christ’s Body is under the species of bread, while His Blood is under the species of wine. Now, however, as His Blood is not in reality separated from His Body, by real concomitance His Blood is under the species of bread together with His Body, and likewise His Body under the species of wine together with His Blood. However, if this sacrament had been consecrated at the time of Christ’s passion, when His Blood was really separated from His Body, then only His Body would have been present under the species of bread, and only His Blood under the species of wine.”144 b) When Christ died on the Cross: “Christ’s Body is the same substance in this sacrament and in its proper species, but not in the same way, because in its proper species it comes into contact with surrounding bodies through its own dimensions, while this does not happen in the sacrament”;145 “In this sacrament, Christ’s Body is not compared with its surroundings by means of its own dimensions, through which bodies touch each other, but rather by means of the dimensions of the species of bread and wine. Therefore, it is these species that are acted upon and are seen, and not the Body of Christ itself.”146 “Therefore, everything that pertains to Christ as He is in Himself can be attributed to Him both in His proper species and as He exists in this sacrament, such as to live, to die, to grieve, to be animate or inanimate [that is, with or without His soul], and so on. However, that which pertains to Christ in relation to extrinsic or exterior bodies can be attributed to Him as He exists in His proper species but not as He is in the sacrament; this includes to be mocked, to be spat on, to be crucified, to be scourged, and so on.”147 “Thus, insofar as Christ is in this sacrament, He cannot suffer, although He can die.”148 “Had this sacrament been celebrated during the three days when Christ was dead, His soul would not have been there, neither by the power of the sacrament nor by real concomitance. However, as ‘Christ, raised from the dead, dies no more’ [Rom 6:9], His soul is now always really united to His Body [and to His Blood].”149 “The same Christ who was on the Cross would have been in the sacrament. However, He died upon the cross, and, therefore, had this sacrament been reserved, He would have also died in it.”150 Saint Thomas affirms this in the argument he cites from authority, that is, just as Christ’s soul leaves His physical Body, “Christ’s soul would not have been under this sacrament, not on account of some failure of the power of the words, but rather because of the way things were in reality.”151

This is because what is proper to this sacrament is to take and bring Christ’s Body and Blood just as they are found, in whatever state they are found.

3. After the Resurrection

If the Mass had been celebrated right at the moment of Christ’s Resurrection, it should be fairly obvious that in that moment, Christ’s soul would have also returned to the sacrament; His Body and His Blood in this sacrament would have also acquired a new glorious and immortal state, just as Christ had at that moment in His proper species and just as He has now in heaven. It is in this way, then, that by the sacrament’s power, the substance of Christ’s Blood is present under the species of wine together with (by the power of natural concomitance) His Body, His Soul, His divinity, and the accidents of His human nature; likewise, the substance of Christ’s Body is present under the species of bread together with His Blood, His Soul, His divinity, and the accidents of His human nature.

This is because what is proper to this sacrament is to take and bring Christ’s Body and Blood just as they are found, in whatever state they are found.

chapters.t: “The new mystery of the new testament”
chapters.h:
“THE NEW MYSTERY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT”

“This sacrament affects in man the effect which Christ’s Passion 153

wrought in the world.”

SAINT THOMAS

At the heart of the Mass we have, on one hand, Christ’s Body and Blood mystically separated because of this sacrament; this is sufficient to have the “the new mystery of the New Testament” that Christ entrusted to His disciples! On the other hand, because of the natural accompaniment of concomitance, Christ’s Blood is found together with His Body, His Body with His Blood, and these along with His Soul, His Divinity, and the other accidents of His human nature. Thus, there is no need to look anywhere else for the essence of the sacrifice, that is, the essence of the Eucharistic immolation.

This particular topic has two aspects: 1) In what part of the Mass is the sacrifice carried out?, and 2) What constitutes or makes up the sacrifice?

We should highlight the admirable efforts of so many illustrious theologians, some of them Doctors of the Church and saints, for even if they didn’t meet with success in their works, they at least prepared the path for those who would come after them, and they helped to develop the judgments of the Church’s Magisterium on these topics.

1. In what part of the Mass is the sacrifice carried out?

As we know, “the two parts which, in a certain sense, go to make up the Mass, namely, the liturgy of the word and the Eucharistic liturgy, are so closely connected with each other that they form but one single act of worship.”154 No one looks for the essence of the sacrifice in the liturgy of the word, but rather in the Eucharistic liturgy, which consists mainly of six actions, namely:

1. The oblation of the bread and the wine in the presentation of the gifts or offertory.

2. The consecration of the Lord’s Body and Blood. 3. The verbal oblation of the Lord’s Body and Blood immediately after the consecration.

4. The Rite of Fraction and Commingling.

“THE NEW MYSTERY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT”

5. The priest’s communion under both species.

6. The distribution of communion to the faithful. It is clear that the essence of the sacrifice of the Mass is not:

in the offertory, which is merely a preparation for the sacrifice, since bread and wine are not the victim of the sacrifice.

in the distribution of communion to the lay Christian faithful, since receiving communion is not a sacrifice, but rather a participation in it.

So our focus centers on the other four actions; the question is, if you will, whether the essence of the sacrifice of the Mass consists solely in the double consecration, or in some other action:

It doesn’t consist in the verbal oblation after the consecration, because this is not carried out in persona Christi.

Nor does it consist in the fraction of the bread, which doesn’t affect the species of wine; with regard to the commingling, it would only be a destruction that falls upon the accidents. Some have imagined that a real destruction of the victim is essentially necessary for the sacrifice; however, although this would be necessary “in the sacrifices of the Old Testament and in the sacrifice of the Cross, it doesn’t follow that we must admit such a destruction in the sacrifice of the Mass, which is a completely singular and sui generis sacrifice; this sacrifice only agrees analogically with the other sacrifices.”155 The destruction in the Mass is merely symbolic or representative.

Similarly, the sacrifice doesn’t consist in the priest’s communion, since this is not a sacrificial action, but rather a participation in the sacrifice.

From these considerations, it follows that the common doctrine is that the essence of the sacrifice consists in the consecration of both species, which is ordered to communion as an integral part.

2. What constitutes or makes up the sacrifice?

Now then, for this reason we must be clear that, in order for there to be a sacrifice:

There doesn’t need to be a change in the Person of Christ (indeed, this is unthinkable);

There is no need for a change in Christ’s Body and Blood;

There doesn’t need to be a physical or virtual immolation of the victim that consists in the destruction of the substances of bread and wine;156 “THE NEW MYSTERY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT”

Nor is Christ reduced to a state of humiliation or annihilation (in statum dicliviorem);157

Nor is He isolated from the material world that surrounds Him, since the species are linked to Him;158

Nor do the words of consecration in themselves lead to Christ’s violent death, as these words don’t have the role of cultellus (a knife);159

Lastly, there is no need to entirely reject the idea of immolation by placing the essence of the sacrifice in the oblation.160

Therefore, the double consecration of both species, ordered to communion as an integral part of the sacrifice, suffices for the representation of the bloody immolation of the cross, in such a way that Christ is mystically or sacramentally immolated in an unbloody fashion and offered by the priest in the Eucharist. Therefore, Saint Thomas affirms that the Eucharist “is confected in the Consecration, in which the sacrifice is offered to God.” 161 As Saint Thomas repeatedly insists: “Christ’s Blood in this sacrament directly represents the passion by which it was shed”; 162 “The Blood, consecrated separately, especially represents Christ’s Passion, in which His Blood was separated from His Body.”163

As we have seen when considering Christ’s different states, mortal and passible, bloodless, lifeless, glorious and immortal, such states “do not enter directly into the nature of the sacrament as such . . . and, above all, they are to be excluded from the Eucharist in its sacrificial aspect.”164

Saint Thomas also says: “Although the whole Christ is present under both species, this is not in vain. First, this is because it represents His Passion, in which the Blood was separated from the Body; this is why the form for the consecration of the Blood makes mention of its shedding. Secondly, it is fitting for the use of this sacrament that Christ’s Body be shown to the faithful as food, and His Blood as drink.” 165 Elsewhere the Angelic Doctor teaches: “If we consider what is only a sign [sacramentum tantum], it is fitting that the Body be signified by means of the species of bread, and the Blood with the species of wine, because this signification indicates a spiritual meal, and a meal properly has both food and drink. . . . If, however, we consider what is both the reality and the sign [res et sacramentum], it is fitting that this sacrament be a remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, which could not be done in a better way than this [with the separate “THE NEW MYSTERY OF THE NEW TESTAMENT”

consecration of the two species], in order to signify His blood as shed and separated from His body.”166

May the “Eucharistic woman,” the Virgin Mary, obtain for us the grace of being able to always imitate her so that we might “eucharistize” our entire lives!

chapters.t: In his proper species and under the sacramental species
chapters.h:
IN HIS PROPER SPECIES AND UNDER THE SACRAMENTAL SPECIES

“God’s life-giving Word, uniting Himself with His own flesh, also made it life-giving. It was fitting therefore that He united Himself to our own bodies through His most holy flesh and precious blood, which 167

we receive in the life-giving blessing in bread and wine.”

SAINT THOMAS

Let us now consider two other notions that Saint Thomas frequently uses in his treatise on the Eucharist, and that is the difference between what he calls in specie propia and in specie sacramenti. In fact, the word species, or its plural form, appears 50 times in the treatise, and so it is clearly a key idea in the Angelic Doctor’s Eucharistic thought.

Let’s first consider these words themselves, then their meanings, and lastly examine the similarities that exist between the two, along with the differences.

1. The Words Themselves

In specie propria: with his characteristic freedom, Saint Thomas uses many words or phrases that are equivalent and also very beautiful, for example:

in sua specie visibili,168 visibili specie,169 sub specie propria,170 in sua specie171 We could go on and on, but, to avoid that, let’s simply consider a text where Saint Thomas gives the reasons why our Lord instituted the Eucharistic sacrifice in an alien species, just before He was going to leave this world. This is because of what is contained in what He was instituting, that is, that it contains Christ sacramentally: “Therefore, when Christ was going to leave His disciples in His proper species, He left Himself with them under the sacramental species, just as in the absence of the emperor his image is set up to be venerated.”172

IN HIS PROPER SPECIES AND UNDER THE SACRAMENTAL SPECIES

Sub aliena specie: this expression is used only a few times.173 The other phrases are used more often:

in sacramentali specie (twice),174 in sacramentali specie, qua est species panis et vini,175 sed specie panis et vini (four times),176 sub utraque specie sacramenti177 These are the words that are used; in other places, Saint Thomas will speak of in propriis dimensionibus, in its own, proper dimensions, or “under foreign dimensions,” following that train of thought as a topic that is intimately linked to this.178

2. The Meaning of These Words

Saint Thomas himself provides us with the meanings: “Christ’s Body is under its own proper species in heaven, and on many altars under the sacramental species.”179 This is what it means.

Later he will also say: “This sacrament contains Christ Himself, though not under His proper species [in specie propria], but rather under the sacramental species [in specie sacramenti].”180 Thus, in his development of the topic, in his response to the first objection, he will give the reason why it is said that men eat the Bread of Angels; the reason is because the possession and enjoyment of Jesus Christ, in specie propria, first and foremost belongs to the angels and saints who delight in seeing Jesus Christ face-to-face in heaven: “The glorified eye always beholds Christ just as He is in His proper species.”181 This is said secondarily of men who delight in Christ sub sacramento and who receive Him in this sacrament. It is here that we find the difference between the two notions.182

3. Differences

First, we must say with complete clarity that the substance of Our Lord’s Body and Blood exists both in specie propria as well as under the specie sacramenti. The difference that we are going to see is with regard to the mode, because in His proper species Christ is present with His accidents; in the foreign or alien species Christ will also be present, but under the sacramental species: He will also have His accidents, but He must have them in a different way. Some texts are as follows: “Christ’s Body is the same substance in this sacrament and in its proper species, but not in the same way, because in its proper species it comes into contact with surrounding bodies through its own dimensions, while this does not happen in the sacrament.”183 This thought has a very interesting application, one that is

IN HIS PROPER SPECIES AND UNDER THE SACRAMENTAL SPECIES

extremely important for us: “Therefore, everything that pertains to Christ as He is in Himself can be attributed to Him both in His proper species and as He exists in this sacrament, such as to live, to die, to grieve, to be animate or inanimate [that is, with or without His soul], and so on. However, that which pertains to Christ in relation to extrinsic or exterior bodies can be attributed to Him as He exists in His proper species but not as He is in the sacrament; this includes to be mocked, to be spat on, to be crucified, to be scourged, and so on.”184

From this it follows that: “Christ’s being in Himself and being in the sacrament are not the same.”185

This difference is also apparent in the consumption of the sacrament: “What is eaten under its proper species is also broken and chewed under its own species; however, Christ’s Body is not eaten under its own species but rather under the sacramental species. Thus Augustine, commenting on Jesus’ words, ‘the flesh is of no avail,’ says ‘This refers to those who understand these things carnally. They understood flesh in the way it is torn to pieces in a cadaver, or as it is sold in the market.’ Christ’s Body, therefore, is not broken except according to the sacramental species. This is the way that Berengarius’s confession is to be understood: the breaking and chewing refers to the sacramental species under which Christ’s Body is truly present.”186

Another characteristic that distinguishes these two notions are their dimensions: under His proper species Christ is present with His own proper dimensions, whereas under the sacramental species He is substantially present with the dimensions of the bread and the wine.187

Yet another difference is that, while under His own species, Christ is visible; under an alien species, however, Christ is invisible, hidden under the species of bread and wine.188 This also applies to His passibility,189 as the Angelic Doctor clearly explains: “It is clear that [at the Last Supper] the same Body that the Apostles saw in its own species [in propria specie] was received by them under the sacramental species [in specie sacramenti]. However, what the Apostles saw in its proper species was not impassible; indeed, it was well-disposed for the passion [Christ had been prepared precisely for the passion], and therefore what they received in the sacrament was not impassible either.”190 The Body that they received in the sacrament was not impassible, but rather passible, capable of suffering. “However, what was in itself passible was present under the sacramental species in an impassible way, just as in this sacrament what is visible in itself is contained invisibly. Just as vision requires contact with the body that is

IN HIS PROPER SPECIES AND UNDER THE SACRAMENTAL SPECIES

seen by means of sight, so does passion require contract of the body that suffers with the agent that inflicts that suffering. In this sacrament, Christ’s Body is not compared with its surroundings by means of its own dimensions, through which bodies touch each other, but rather by means of the dimensions of the species of bread and wine. Therefore, it is these species that are acted upon and are seen, and not Christ’s Body itself.”191

As we will see later, this is linked with difference that there is between Christ’s proper species and alien species with respect to whether or not Christ is present in a localized way, that is, what is the movement of Christ’s body; how is His definite presence related to the circumscriptive presence, which is not the sort of presence He has in this sacrament.

In the same way, this reality marks the difference between the sacrifice of the Cross and its perpetuation in the sacrifice of the Mass: the latter is an unbloody, sacramental, and mystical sacrifice.192 Saint Thomas will express it in these words: “Since this sacrament is a sign of Christ’s passion, and not the passion itself, it is fitting that the suffering signified by the ‘fractio’ not be of Christ’s Body, but rather of the species that signify it.”193

There are priests who, as we saw in the Second Book of Maccabees, have forgotten the sacrifice of the altar. May we not be counted among them, and may we never forget that what is most important in our lives is the altar, the Eucharist, the Lord in this sacrament. Let us renew, always and in a particular way in this year of the Eucharist, our desires to fulfill our duty in the best way possible, because, as the holy Curé of Ars remarked, “The reason why a priest becomes lazy is because he doesn’t give enough attention to the Mass.”194

chapters.t: On account of the sacrament and on account of concomitance
chapters.h:
ON ACCOUNT OF THE SACRAMENT AND ON ACCOUNT OF CONCOMITANCE

“The Blood, soul, and divinity are not present in the Eucharist in the same way that the Body of Christ is present. Pastors, however, should not fail to observe that in this Sacrament not all these things are contained after the same manner, or by the same power. Some things, we say, are present in virtue of the consecration; for as the words of consecration effect what they signify, sacred writers usually say that whatever the form expresses, is contained in the Sacrament by virtue of the Sacrament. Hence, could we suppose any one thing to be entirely separated from the rest, the Sacrament, they teach, would be found to contain solely what the form expresses and nothing more. On the other hand, some things are contained in the Sacrament because they are united to those which are expressed in the form. For instance, the words ‘This is My Body,’ which comprise the form used to consecrate the bread, signify the body of the Lord, and hence the body itself of Christ the Lord is contained in the Eucharist by virtue of the Sacrament. Since, however, to Christ’s body are united His blood, His soul, and

His Divinity, all of these also must be found to coexist in the Sacrament; not, however, by virtue of the consecration, but by virtue of the union that subsists between them and His body. All these are said to be in the Eucharist by virtue of concomitance. Hence it is clear that

Christ, whole and entire, is contained in the Sacrament; for when two 195 things are actually united, where one is, the other must also be.”

THE ROMAN CATECHISM

I was thinking about how whenever we study Saint Thomas, we can always take away some conclusion. One of these conclusions is how our study of theology, and in particular of the Eucharist, has huge gaps. You come to realize this when Saint Thomas says “patet” (“it is evident”) and it’s certainly not evident for you, who have a mixture of other thoughts and ideas in mind. The same happens when Saint Thomas says, “manifestum est,” “it’s unmistakable,” and, yet, it’s not so unmistakable for us; maybe we’ve never heard these things, and we celebrate Mass every day! But, either they never taught us these things, or we didn’t learn them, or we didn’t study them, or we didn’t delve into them more deeply, or we didn’t pray, or we didn’t remember them or . . . any number of things.

We’ve already seen how the Eucharist is both a sacrament and a sacrifice. Then we saw how Jesus instituted it as food and drink, and how He is in His proper species and how He is under the sacramental, that is, alien, species. Now, God willing, let’s see how Jesus’ presence in the Eucharist is two-fold: He’s there by the sacrament’s power, ex vi sacramenti, but also ex vi concomitantiae, by means of accompaniment or concomitance.

Before beginning on this topic, though, we need to make a clarification about what we’ve seen so far with regard to “in His proper species” and “under an alien species”: these two things aren’t exactly equal, meaning they don’t have the exact same importance, and this is because “under the species of bread and wine” always has a relation and a connection with “in His own, proper species,” which has priority.

The same happens with the other notions that Saint Thomas often uses. I’ve come to discover them just now: in some cases, he uses the word directe, directly, or per se, in order to make reference to the vi sacramenti. Sometimes, when speaking of the vi concomitantiae, he says quasi per accidens, 196 meaning that there’s not a strict equality or equivalence between the two ways in which the Lord becomes present in the Eucharist.

Another curious thing with Saint Thomas, something that we know but that often we don’t come to see or think about, is how he moves his train of thought and progresses with great surety. This is because he always keeps in mind, first and foremost and as a sure starting point, the dogmas of faith. After these, he uses the surety of the facts of experience. The expressions that he uses here recall the beginning of each one of his vias: these ways always begin from an fact of sense experience, something that is really irrefutable. 197 The same is true of this treatise on the Eucharist.

This is the way that question 76 begins: “It is absolutely necessary to confess, according to the Catholic faith, that the entire Christ is in this sacrament.”198 This “being in” of the entire Christ is in two ways: ex vi sacramenti and ex naturali concomitantia.

1. Why? What’s the reason for Our Lord to have a second mode of presence in the Eucharist?

Manifestum est, replies the Angelic Doctor. He uses this phrase in an objection that he raises, and so usually we don’t give it much importance. However, he uses it in the affirmation in the objection, and then, later, in the reply to that objection, he uses the same phrase: “It is evident [manifestum est] that neither bread nor wine can be converted into Christ’s soul or divinity.”199 This is what he says in the first objection, and also in the reply to it: “Since the change of the bread and the wine does not end in the divinity or in Christ’s soul, it follows that Christ’s soul and divinity are not in this sacrament by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti], but rather on account of real concomitance [ex reali concomitantia].”200 He continues explaining in the same reply: “As the divinity never laid aside the assumed Body, wherever Christ’s Body is, His divinity must necessarily be there as well. Hence, His divinity must necessarily accompany His Body in this sacrament.” 201 The Latin text reads “His divinity must necessarily . . . concomitantem eius corpus,” because the divinity never abandoned the Lord’s Body, not even when He was in the tomb, not even when He descended to Abraham’s bosom, the limbo of the just. Elsewhere Saint Thomas says, “Something is present in this sacrament in another way by real concomitance, as the Divinity of the Word, which is in the sacrament by the indissoluble union that it has with Christ’s Body, as the substance of bread could in no way be converted into the divinity.”202

With respect to Christ’s soul, we see the different states that it had when it was separated from the Lord’s Body after He died on the cross until He resurrected on the third day; however, Christ risen from the dead dies no more, and thus wherever Christ’s Body is now, His soul must be as well, because in the Eucharist Christ is whole and entire. This is a truth of the faith.

In his Commentary on the Sentences, Saint Thomas explained even more: “Something is contained in the sacrament of the altar in two ways: one way is by the power of the sacrament [ex vi sacramenti] and the other by natural concomitance. By the sacrament’s power, what is contained is that in which the change ends, and what this is can be known in three ways. First, where the change ends can be known by that which has been converted or changed, for the matter of the sacraments isn’t changed except insofar as it has some similitude, according to its nature, to that into which it is changed, like wine into Blood. Secondly, the end can be known according to the meaning of the form, by whose power the change takes place; thus it follows that the change ends in that which is signified or meant by the form. Thirdly, the end can be known by the use of the sacrament, as that which pertains to food is contained under the species of bread by the sacrament’s power, and that which pertains to drink, under the species of wine. Nonetheless, by natural concomitance, and ‘quasi per accidens,’ the sacrament contains everything which, by itself, is not the end of the change, but without which the end of the change cannot be reached.”203

In other words, according to the Angelic Doctor, there are three reasons by which we know ex vi sacramenti, that is, by the sacrament’s power, what is the end or result of the change:

1. By the a quo and ad quem ends (the beginning and end of the change), which should have a certain similitude with each other.

2. By the meaning of the words of the sacrament. 3. By the use of the sacrament, that is, what the sacrament is destined for.

For these reasons, the end of the change is neither Christ’s soul nor His divinity: “Accordingly, therefore, it is evident, as Christ’s soul has no similarity with the substance of bread, and the sacramental form makes no mention of His soul, and His soul is not properly ordered to the use of the sacrament [nec anima conveniat ad usum sacramenti], which is to be eaten and drunk, that the change of the bread and wine does not properly end in Christ’s soul, but rather in His Body and Blood which are not separated from His soul. Thus, Christ’s soul is not contained in this sacrament by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti], but rather by natural concomitance with the Body that the soul animates.”204

Saint Thomas continues, explaining the minimum necessary for the words of consecration to be true: “The soul is the form of the body, giving it the whole order of perfect being, that is, corporeal being, animated being, and so forth. Accordingly, the form of bread is changed into the form of Christ’s Body insofar as it gives corporeal being, but not insofar as gives being animated by the soul.”205

Elsewhere he further develops the fact that it is not by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti] that Christ’s Blood is contained under the species of bread and His Body under the species of wine: “As this sacrament was instituted for the use of the faithful, it follows that there is something in this sacrament that is directed to the use of the faithful that comes about by the sacrament’s power itself. Hence, as the consecrated bread doesn’t contain Christ’s Blood as drink for the faithful [but rather contains Christ’s Body to be consumed as food], it follows that Christ’s Blood is not contained under the species of bread by the sacrament’s power, but rather by natural concomitance, since it is not fitting for Christ’s Body to be without His Blood; and the reverse is true for the consecrated wine. Hence, it is not by reason of the very first words [of the consecration of the bread] that the bread is converted into Christ’s Body and Blood, but rather, by these words, it is converted into the Body without Blood, which will come to be consumed as drink by the faithful.”206

Aquinas gives a two-fold reason why the Blood should be consecrated separately from the Body: first, because nourishment consists of both eating and drinking, and, secondly, because the Eucharist perfectly represents the Lord’s Passion. As the Angelic Doctor writes: “The reason, then, why the Blood is consecrated separately from the Body, even though the two are not currently separated, can be considered, on one hand, from the use of the sacrament, the reason why it exists: nourishment consists in both food and drink. On the other hand, it can be considered with regard to what is represented in the sacrament, because in the Passion Christ’s Blood was separated from His Body.”207

However, an interesting difficulty arises: what has already been done cannot be done again. Christ’s Body has already started to be present in the sacrament by the consecration of the bread. So, it cannot be that it starts to be present by the consecration of the wine. To this, Thomas replies: “Christ’s Body is not under the species of wine by the sacrament’s power, but rather by real concomitance. In the same manner, Christ’s Body doesn’t become present by itself through the consecration of the wine, but rather concomitantly.”208

In fact, if someone where to consecrate only one species, it would be an imperfect sacrifice, and the defect would have to be remedied.209

2. What does one mode do, and how about the other?

Ex vi sacramenti, the sacramental power, produces what is under the sacramental species, that is, what the substances of bread and wine are directly [directe] converted into: the

Lord’s Body and Blood. The substances of bread and wine cease to exist, being converted into the substance of the Lord’s Body and Blood, which is what is signified or meant by the words of the sacramental form; those words are efficacious (they cause or affect what they signify),210 and so sometimes this power is called ex vi verborum. Dom Vonier says that there are three terms which equally express this reality, though each with their own particular emphasis: by ex vi conversione, which is the transubstantion, “less is represented than by vi verborum, because the words of consecration may mean something more than body and blood.” 211 For instance, those words signify a banquet: Take and eat . . . Take and drink; they also mean a sacrifice and the sacramental state of the victim: which will be given up . . . which will be poured out. The words point to a sacrifice of propitiation: for the forgiveness of sins. Both expressions “are contained under the more comprehensive expression vi sacramenti.”212

Ex naturali concomitantia (meaning, because of natural concomitance, connection, or company): this is what is really united to what becomes present here by means of the change; it means what is really united to what makes up the ad quem end of the change.213 Saint Thomas adds a reflection which carries a great deal of importance: “If two things are really united, then wherever one really is, it is necessary for the other one to be there as well, since things that are really united with each other are only distinguishable by an operation of the soul.”214

3. The Names

We’ve had the chance to examine Christ’s two different modes of presence in the Eucharist. Saint Thomas uses different expressions in order to refer to each of them. With respect to the first, he uses:

ex vi sacramenti, quasi ex vi sacramenti,215 ex vi verborum,216 ex vi conversionis, ex vi sacramenti,217 per se,218 directe ex vi sacramenti219 With respect to the other notion, ex vi concomitantiae, he almost always uses two adjectives in order to emphasize that this is not simply a question that he happened to think up, as many times happens to us, piously, when we’re going through a meditation; rather, this concomitance is something real:

ex reali concomitantia,220 ex naturali concomitantia,221 and elsewhere he writes quasi ex quadam concomitantia222 (making it clear elsewhere that this is not something per se).223

Other expressions he uses are: quasi per accidens, concomitanter,224 and non fit . . . per se.225

4. What of Christ is present in the Eucharist under each of the two modes of presence? · a) Ex vi sacramenti:

What is present ex vi sacramenti is only that at which the change directly ends, that is, the substance of Christ’s Body under the appearance of bread, and the substance of Christ’s Blood under the species of wine. By means of the double consecration, the sacramental state of the victim also comes about.

Christ’s Blood is not under the species of bread; neither are His soul and His divinity present.

Christ’s Body is not under the species of wine; neither are His soul and His divinity present.

b) Ex vi concomitantiae:

By this mode, what is present is everything that is united to the substance of Christ’s Body and Blood. Under the appearance of bread, we have Christ’s Blood, Soul, Divinity, dimensive quantity–which never really separates from the substance–and all the other accidents because of concomitance. Under the appearance of wine, we have the Body, Soul, Divinity, dimensive quantity, and all the other accidents.

Now let us consider two texts from Saint Thomas: “Its dimensive quantity is there concomitantly and, as it were, accidentally [quasi per accidens] and not according to its proper mode, but rather after the manner of substance.”226 In the same way, that is, ex vi concomitantiae, Christ’s different states (except His victimal state) are present. Accordingly, in His earthly life (the Last Supper), He was found in the Eucharist in a passible state; from the moment of His death until His resurrection, hypothetically there would have been a corresponding state where His soul was separated from His Body. From His Resurrection even until now, He is in His glorious and immortal state.

We said “except His victimal state,” because Christ is always present in a sacramental victimal state by means of the double consecration. Those other states were accidents of Christ’s Body, and so didn’t pertain to the substance of

Christ’s Body. This is why the distinction between the two modes of Christ’s presence in the Eucharist is a very important doctrine. Sometimes we have difficulties understanding how the Mass is a sacrifice; we can say, “But, how, if Christ has already risen?” However, the Church’s doctrine, as the Council of Trent says, is that, by means of the sacrament, Christ’s Blood appears separated from His Body, and that is the Eucharistic sacrifice. That Christ is now in His resurrected state, just as He is now in heaven, is something that must logically be held, because this sacrament makes Christ’s Body and Blood present; whatever state Christ’s Body might be in at that moment doesn’t affect the sacramental reality.

In the second text, Saint Thomas responds to a difficulty that arises from the state of Christ’s Body on the altar, comparing it with the state in which it was found upon the table of the Last Supper, considering those states are accidents of the Body: “The accidents of Christ’s Body are in this sacrament by real concomitance, and not by the sacrament’s power, for by this only the substance of Christ’s Body [and Blood] come to be there. Thus, the power of the sacramental words extends to making Christ’s Body present, whatever might be the accidents that really exist in it.”227

In accord with their heretical doctrines, sacramental Protestants–such as Carlostad, Zwingli, Oecolampadius, and many others–mocked the doctrine of concomitance: Martin Luther ridiculed it, and Melanchthon pretended not to know of it when he says that some people torment themselves with vain reasoning.228 In this age of false ecumenism and the influence of Protestant thought on Catholic thinkers, some theologians have become accomplices and followers of these doctrines.

They, like so many others, forget the Council of Trent’s clear teaching: “For the Apostles had not yet received the Eucharist from the hands of the Lord [cfr. Mt 26:26; Mk 14:22], when He Himself told them that what He was giving them is His own body. This has always been the belief of the Church of God . . . [that] the body [is present] under the form of bread and the blood under the form of wine ex vi verborum but the same body also under the form of wine and the same blood under the form of bread and the soul under both, in virtue of that natural connection and concomitance.”229 To forget this carries dreadful consequences.

Although this distinction between what is found in the Eucharist “by the power of the words” and what is there “by concomitance” is perhaps not a dogma of faith, it would, nevertheless, be erroneous and reckless to deny it, not only because the authority of the Council of Trent employs those very expressions in order to clarify the mystery, but also because the distinction that we are speaking of here is clearly derived from the principles of the faith. 230 In fact, the paragraph in which the Council of Trent teaches, among other things, that distinction, begins by stating: “It has always been a firm belief in the Church of God.” It would seem that the Catechism of the Catholic Church maintains the same doctrine, as some 11 times it uses the expressions “words” 231 or “conversion”232 referring to Christ’s Body and Blood contained under the species of bread and wine; it would seem to refer to concomitance by using the synonym “together” in order to refer to Christ’s soul and divinity.233

chapters.t: By way of substance – by way of quantity
chapters.h:
BY WAY OF SUBSTANCE – BY WAY OF QUANTITY

“It is clear that it is not the dimensions of bread and wine

that are changed in the dimensions of Christ’s Body, 234

but rather substance into substance.”

SAINT THOMAS

Now we’ll concern ourselves with two additional terms that Saint Thomas uses quite often in his treatise on the Eucharist, and these terms are per modum substantiae and per modum quantitatis. As often happens in Saint Thomas’s works, these terms are related to two others: dimensiones alienate, and propriae dimensiones.235 Here we can see, as we have already had the opportunity to affirm, Saint Thomas’s fidelity in respecting both what he says with regard to faith and to reason. Each time that the Angelic Doctor goes to make a theological advance, he will do so by basing himself on an article of faith or by rooting himself in some fact of experience, and here we have three instances in which he makes reference to (and bases his argumentation on) facts of experience. Sometimes, we just let these things pass us by, or we understand them only superficially; hence, we don’t reach the full depth of Saint Thomas’s theological thought, and we are left without understanding why he says this or that thing: everything is half clouded over.

In the corpus of question 75, referring to the accidents of the Eucharist, Saint Thomas will say: “quod sensu apparet,” “as it appears to the senses”236 the accidents of bread and wine remain. Each and every day we must affirm that, as Saint Augustine says: “Under the species of bread and wine, which we see, we honor the Body and Blood which we do not see.”237 Continuing, Aquinas affirms that it is this way because God has wanted it to be so: “Divine Providence has reasonably done this.” Although it doesn’t enter directly into the topic that we are examining here, it is worthwhile to recall, because Saint Thomas explains it very well, that the accidents remain for the following three reasons: “[1] it is not usual . . . for men to eat human flesh and drink human blood. . . . [2] So that the sacrament might not be mocked or made fun of by unbelievers. . . . [3] When we consume our Lord’s Body and Blood invisibly, this increases the merits of our faith.”238 In the first place, then, it is a question of what our senses themselves tell us: after the Consecration, the species or accidents of bread and wine remain; these species are everything that is perceivable by the senses, such as extension, size, weight, color, figure, texture, smell, taste, sound (the breaking of the bread produces the same sound before and after consecration).239

In the question that follows, where Saint Thomas deals directly with the topic that we are seeing now, he returns to say the same thing in the first article: “It is clear that it is not the dimensions of bread and wine that are changed in the dimensions of the Body of Christ, but rather substance into substance.” 240 If the accidents remain, which is patet, then it is also evident that the accident of dimensive quantity remains, an accident, not of the Body, but rather of the bread and wine. This change is from substance to substance, that of bread into the substance of Christ’s Body and that of wine into Christ’s Blood, and not of the dimensions. Thus, the Body and Blood are present ex vi sacramenti, but the dimensions, that is, the quantitative dimensions of the Body and Blood, are not present in this way. These dimensions are there only ex vi realis concomitantiae and hence in the mode of substance (following upon substance).

Returning, then, to our question: unde patet (once again, a return to the reality of the senses) that if the accidents remain, among those accidents is dimensive quantity, which remains the same both before and after consecration: “It is clear that it is not the dimensions of bread and wine that are changed in the dimensions of Christ’s Body, but rather substance into substance. Thus, the substance of Christ’s Body or Blood is in this sacrament ex vi sacramenti; the same is not true, however, for the dimensions of

Christ’s Body or Blood. Hence, it is clear that Christ’s Body is present in this sacrament by way of substance, and not by way of quantity.”241 This reasoning is very clear, and this is what has been clearly taught since the Council of Trent. It is what Paul VI recalled in Mysterium Fidei242 against Schillebeeckx’s denials. This is what Saint Thomas explains so beautifully: Christ is present by way of substance: “Hence, it is clear that Christ’s Body is present in this sacrament by way of substance [per modum substantiae], and not by way of quantity [per modum quantitatis]. However, the particular totality of a substance is indifferently or equally contained in a small or large quantity [a drop of water is water, but so is an immense ocean]. . . . Thus, the entire substance of Christ’s Body and Blood are contained in this sacrament after consecration, just as the substances of bread and wine were contained before consecration.”243

241 S. Th., III, q. 76, a. 1, ad 3: “Ex quo patet quod dimensiones panis vel vini non convertuntur in dimensiones Corporis Christi, sed substantia in substantiam.

Summarizing, then, we have three evident conclusions that are all connected:

1. It is evident that the accidents of bread and wine remain.

2. Therefore, it is evident that what is changed is only the substance of bread and wine; there is no change or conversion with respect to the accidents.

3. Consequently, it is clear that dimensions of Christ’s Body and Blood are not present by way of quantity (the Blood alone would be some six liters), but rather by way of substance and by concomitance.

Thus, Christ’s Body is not present by way of dimensive quantity: it cannot be measured or counted out; hence, in this sacrament, Christ’s Body is not localized.244 This is a consequence of being present by way of substance. “The substance of Christ’s Body is linked with a place through foreign dimensions [and not its own dimensions] and thus, on the contrary, His proper dimensions are connected with that place by way of substance, which is contrary to the notion of a localized body; therefore, in no way is Christ’s Body present in this sacrament in a localized way.”245

Saint Thomas raises a difficulty connected with this: “To be definitively or circumscriptively in a place is to be localized. However, Christ’s Body seems to be definitively in this sacrament, because it is where the species of bread and wine are and therefore not on other parts of the altar. Likewise, Christ’s Body seems to be circumscriptively present, because it is contained under the consecrated host’s species, which it neither goes beyond and which do not go beyond the Body. Thus, Christ’s Body is in the sacrament as in a place.”246 To this he responds: “Christ’s Body is not definitively present in this sacrament; if it were, then it would be only on that altar where the sacrament was being confected. Rather, it is present under its own species in heaven, and on many altars under sacramental species. Likewise, it is clear that it is not present in this sacrament circumscriptively, as Christ’s Body is not present according to the measure of its own quantity, as was said earlier. That Christ’s Body is not outside of the sacrament’s superficies, nor on some other part of the altar, does not pertain to being there definitively or circumscriptively, but rather to the fact that it is there by the consecration and change of the bread and wine, as was already stated.”247

That is, Christ’s presence doesn’t come about in this sacrament in a definitive and limited way, nor is it a circumscriptive presence that measures the dimensions of the place.

Let’s clarify further: this circumscriptive presence is that “by which a thing is in a place by the adaptation and commensuration of that thing’s own quantity with the dimensions of that place, in such a way that its entirety is entirely in that place and, with that thing’s parts, it is in the parts of that place,”248 which is something that doesn’t take place in the Eucharist.

Nor does it happen that the Eucharistic presence in a place (ubi) is in a definitive, that is, local and limited, way, meaning the way of presence in which “the thing is present in a place in such a way that it is not in some other place at the same time.”249

Christ is present in the Eucharist in totally unique and inexpressible manner: He is sacramentally present. What does this mean? It means that Christ’s Body, in its proper species, is in heaven, and, at the same time, it is present on many altars under sacramental species. 250 This is why Saint Thomas says that “Christ’s Body is present [in this sacrament] in a way that is proper to this sacrament.”251

Saint Thomas repeatedly teaches that, because Christ’s Body is present in the Eucharist in specie sacramenti, it is present per modum substantiae, and not in the manner of quantity:

“If its [the substance of Christ’s Body’s] dimensive quantity is also present, this happens accidently, as it were, and by concomitance. This would not be according to the proper manner of quantity, namely, that the whole is in the whole, and the parts are in the parts, but rather according to the manner of substance, the nature of which is for the whole to be in the whole, and the whole in every individual part.”252

“Thus it is clear that Christ’s Body is present in the sacrament by way of substance, and not by way of quantity.”253

“Christ’s Body is present in this sacrament substantively, that is, in the way in which a substance is under its dimensions; it is not present in the way of dimensions, that is, the way in which the dimensive quantity of some body is under the dimensive quantity of place.”254

“[Christ’s Body] is present after the manner of substance, as we have said.”255

“Christ’s Body is not present in this sacrament in the way that is proper to dimensive quantity, but according to the manner of substance.”256 “As was said above, Christ’s Body is present in this sacrament substantially.”257

This doctrine has several implications. Saint Thomas then asks: “Since Christ’s Body is an organic body, there is a fixed distance between each of its parts . . . like the distance of one eye to the other, or from the eyes to the ears. However, if the whole of Christ were present under each part of the species, then every part of Christ would be under every part of the species, and thus where one part is, the other part would be there too.”258 To this, the Angelic Doctor responds: “Such an argument refers to the nature of bodies insofar as they have dimensive quantity, but, as we have already said, Christ’s Body is not present in the manner of quantity, but rather in the manner of substance.”259

This is really something quite fascinating, which we have only superficially examined. Even the great theologians have remained entranced in the face of this reality, as they see how God has brought about the mystery of the Eucharist in a way that is absolutely unthinkable for the human mind. Even after divine revelation, we find ourselves with many things that clearly surpass our capacity to understand, because God clearly surpasses us. One theologian, Toledo, said: “God can do much more than man can understand or even imagine. Indeed, if an expert can do many things that the peasant, because of his ignorance, can neither understand nor even imagine, how could God be unable to do many more things than what a created intellect or imagination can conceive of? It’s foolish, then, to attempt to measure God’s knowledge by our intelligence, for His knowledge is infinitely beyond a created intellect, far, far more than that created intellect is distant from that of a peasant or from the imagination of an irrational animal. . . . Humility is necessary for this mystery, humility which coexists with faith, but which alone cannot reach prefect and clear knowledge.”260 This is how it is with God, since we are all more than simple in front of Him. He wanted to do some marvelous things in this sacrament of the Eucharist, like this singular, ineffable, unique manner of being present per modum substantiae.

CHRIST WHO SUFFERED

“The Eucharist is the sacrament of Christ’s Passion, 261 for man is made perfect in union with Christ who suffered.”

SAINT THOMAS

1. Some Citations

The Greek Fathers of the Church didn’t use a phrase that corresponds exactly to the Latin passus, that is, to the perfect participle; rather, they made use of two analogous formulas: the verbal adjective παθητóς (translated as suffering or, perhaps better, able to suffer) and the aorist participle πάθων, οντος. Nevertheless, in these expressions (particularly in the last one) we see a tendency to attribute Christ’s passion as a characteristic proper to Him, almost as a sort of epithet. Thus, for example, in the ancient homily In sanctum Pascha: “For in all things prophesized about Christ who suffered [τοῦ Χριστοῦ παθόντος], it was necessary. . . . ” 262 Saint John

Damascene wrote, “We are taught of Christ who suffered in His very flesh [Χριστὸν δὲ παθόντα σαρκὶ ἐδιδάχθημεν].”263

There are also texts from the Latin Fathers and other authors that tend to reinforce this idea. We cite only a few examples:

“Who would not see the sufferings of Christ from His own nation denoted by Noah being drunk with the wine of the vineyard he planted, and his being uncovered in his tent?”264

“And thus Moses was a figure of the Jewish people, who would later come to believe in Christ who suffered.”265

“Now infants are strangers to this salvation and light . . . unless they are joined to the people of God by adoption, holding to Christ who suffered the just for the unjust, to bring them unto God.”266

“The substance of the psalm [69] is that Christ has suffered [Christus passus] according to the frailty of human nature.”267

“What else could the roasted fish mean but Christ who suffered?”268 “For, what does that baked fish, eaten by Christ after the Resurrection and given Him by the disciples, mean other than Christ Himself who suffered [Christum passum]?”269 “That is, they honored Him by believing rightly, and by worthily partaking of the sacraments of Christ who suffered [Christi passi].”270

The Synod of Arras (1025) also alludes to the bodily presence of Christus passus: “Indeed, although Christ suffered only once and although He has died only once, every day He suffers for us in the Church, and every day His memorial is brought about for our good.”271

The expression takes on a very precise, almost technical, meaning in Saint Thomas’s works, and in particular in the treatise on the Eucharist: “The Eucharist is the sacrament of Christ’s Passion, for man is made perfect in union with Christ who suffered [Christum passum].”272

“The Eucharist is the perfect sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, insofar as it contains Christ Himself who suffered [Christum passum].”273

“All of the Old Testament sacrifices were figures with respect to Christ who was crucified [Christum passum], who is contained in this sacrament.”274 “It was fitting, then, that the sacrifice of the New Law, instituted by Christ, should have something more. It should contain the very Christ who suffered [ipsum passum], and not only in meaning or figure, but rather in truth.”275 “With respect to what is sign and reality [id quod est res et sacramentum], the figure contained in the law of Moses was more expressive [than the sacrifice of Melchizedek] inasmuch as Christ who suffered [Christus passus] was more expressly prefigured in it.”276 “Since this sacrament [the Eucharist] is the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, it contains in itself Christ who suffered [Christum passum].”277

2. Some considerations from a grammatical standpoint

Before considering the expression Christus passus itself, there are two expressions that we should examine, both of which are related to our topic and which are quite interesting in themselves. These expressions are Body given up and Blood shed. In the words of the institution of the Eucharist, Our Lord gives us the truth that the Eucharist contains His Body given up (cf. Lk 22:19) and His shed Blood (cf. Mt 26:28, Mk 14:24, Lk 22:20). In the Greek text of the New Testament, these two qualities are expressed with present participles (διδόμενον meaning given up, and ἐκχὖννόμενον meaning shed). Now then, classical languages have verbal systems that do not always match up with each other. For example, Greek verbs have what are called aspects, which Latin has less of. This means that in Greek, sometimes the tense of a verb does not actually have a temporal value (meaning present, past, or future), although many times it does, above all in the indicative mood. What the tenses of Greek verbs do is indicate a characteristic (an aspect) of the action.

For instance, the present tense in Greek indicates an element of continuity, that is, of the duration of an action. The way in which this aspect of the present affects that continuity is highly debated by grammarians of Greek, and this is not relevant to our concerns.279 It is enough that we understand from this that these two present participles used by Our Lord do not primarily mean the present tense, but rather the aspect of continuation or of duration.

Furthermore, in New Testament Greek the present participle is used with a future meaning, especially when referring to something in the imminent future.280

We can conclude, then, that the present participles given up and shed used by Jesus in the institution of the Eucharist show that they refer to His Body that will be given up and His Blood that will be shed the following day during the Passion. However, these participles also and necessarily include the very moment of their institution (that is, the Last Supper), and also the continuation or perpetuation of that action throughout the centuries, that is, the sacrifice of the Mass. At the Last Supper, there was Blood shed and a Body given up, though not in a bloody way. The same happens at Mass. In fact, Jesus’ command to His Apostles, Do this in memory of Me (Lk 22:19, 1 Cor 11:23-24) is also given with a present imperative (ποιεῖτε meaning Do) which is why what Christ instituted at the Last Supper must be continuously repeated. This is also the reason why many good exegetes emphasize the particular strength of these two present participles.281

Turning to the Latin expression that Saint Thomas uses, we see, from the grammatical standpoint, passus is the perfect participle of the verb patior, which means to suffer. The verb is deponent, that is, it has a passive form but an active meaning.

This characteristic form of deponent verb is, we could say, what is most visible about them, but it is neither their only nor most important feature, since often the use of such verbs implies certain nuances that are more adequately and accurately expressed with the passive form rather than with the active. I believe that such is the case with this participle. Indeed, the form passus, insofar as it is the perfect participle of a deponent verb, has various dimensions in its meaning:

It indicates an action that was carried out and completed in the past, that is, it refers to a completed action.

Furthermore, the past participle in Latin is often employed with a present meaning, especially with regard to verbs that indicate some sort of condition of the subject,282 be they mental or physical, as is the case with patior. In this sense, the past participle of a deponent verb can be used in order to indicate an existing state, or to express simultaneity, that is, something present.283

Additionally, the past participle, as a verbal adjective, indicates an attribute of the subject, that is, it attributes the expressed quality of the verb to the subject as something that belongs or pertains to it.284

3. Interpretations of Christus passus

The following interpretations are incorrect:

Some affirm that Christ suffers now: “Indeed, some have said that ‘Christus passus’ means nothing other than Christ suffering, in such a way that Saint Thomas’s words, ‘the Eucharist contains Christus passus’ mean: the Eucharist contains Christ, who suffers now. Although He suffers in a hidden and sacramental way, He is truly suffering in act now.”285 “Others have taught that what these words mean is that which Christ suffered in the past, in such a way Saint Thomas’s words would mean that the Eucharist contains Christ who suffered in the past, but who is no longer present under the state of His passion.”286

The correct interpretation is as follows:

It is the Christus passus who is contained in the Eucharist: “The Eucharist is the perfect sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, in as much as it contains Christ Himself who has suffered [Christum passum]; thus it could not be instituted before the Incarnation, and so [at that time] there was only a place for sacraments that were a prefiguration of the Lord’s Passion.”287

It was prefigured in the Old Testament by the paschal lamb, particularly inasmuch as this lamb was immolated: “All of the Old Testament sacrifices were figures with respect to Christ who was crucified [Christum passum], who is contained in this sacrament, but especially the sacrifice of expiation, which was the most sacred of them all. . . . The paschal lamb . . . prefigured this sacrament . . . as it was immolated by the whole multitude of the children of Israel on the fourteenth day of the new moon, and, as such, as a figure of

Christ’s passion, since Christ is called the Lamb because of His innocence.”288

It is the res et sacramentum: “Since this sacrament [the Eucharist] is the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, it contains in itself Christ who suffered [Christum passum].”289

It must be said that “justly, then, is the sacramental Christ called ‘Christ who has suffered’ [Christus passus] because, in accord with the order established by God, Christ’s real presence under one and the other species does not come about unless Christ becomes present in the state of His passion; as we have said, in virtue of the words [ex vi verborum] only Christ’s Body becomes present under the species of bread, and under the species of wine, only Christ’s Blood.”290

“Thus, just as the sacrament of the Eucharist really and truly contains Jesus Christ, in the same way it contains Christ who has suffered, Body and Blood, violently separated from each other on the Cross for our salvation. There the res et sacramentum of the Eucharist are to be found. It is a reality that, in turn, is signified by a sensible sign (signum tantum). It is by means of the sensible sign that a deeper reality is both symbolized and caused: the sacramental grace of communion and the sacrificial application of the meritorious and satisfactory power of the Cross. Thus, we always return to the crystallized sacrifice, and this is necessary; otherwise, we run the risk of not finding a true sacrifice on the altar, a sacrifice identical to that of the Cross, with the same offerer and the same victim.”291

Summarizing:

Applying the grammatical points we saw earlier with respect to the expression Christus passus, an almost idiomatic expression used by Saint Thomas to refer to the reality contained in the Eucharist, we can conclude that this expression indicates, on one hand, that the entirety of Christ’s redemptive passion can be found therein, including the fruits and merits that our Lord obtained for us: this refers to the complete work of the redemption (this is proper to the perfect tense). On the other hand, the past of the past participle indicates that Christ has already suffered in His flesh, and this only once, on Calvary, and thus the Mass is a relative sacrifice, a commemorative sign of the sacrifice of Calvary. The present meaning of the perfect participle nevertheless indicates that that sacrifice, which took place in the past, is perpetuated; it becomes present, although in a different way (in the sacramental mode). Lastly, it means that that mode of becoming present, that being contained as something ‘suffered’ in the Eucharist, is something proper and exclusive to Christ, just as His unique and only sacrifice is exclusive to Him.

We can ask ourselves why Saint Thomas, if he wanted to indicate the reality of the actual presence of Christ’s sacrifice in the Eucharist, never uses (at least in the questions dedicated to the Eucharist in the Summa Theologica) the present form of the participle (patiens, suffering). A first reason, taken simply from grammar, is that the present participle indicates an action that is actually taking place, actually unfolding, and, consequently, it does not imply the end or perfection (in the sense of being ended or finished) of the work.

More than this, however, is that the present participle could also give rise to erroneous interpretations, as if Christ were suffering in the flesh, that is, in a bloody way, at each Mass. For this reason, the present participle is a less fitting expression to indicate the fact that Christ offers Himself in the Mass in a way different from the way of Calvary, even though they are one and the same sacrifice. In other words: the present participle patiens could be interpreted as Christ actually suffering on the altar. What happens in reality, though, is that Christ becomes present with His unique and only sacrifice which was offered only once in the past but which is perpetuated in every Mass. This sense, the passive, past form is more apt for expressing that Christ offers Himself in every Mass in a different way (that is, sacramentally, in specie aliena), and not in a bloody manner (as happened on Calvary, in specie propia). It is, nevertheless, the same Christ and His one and the same sacrifice.

I think that it is in this sense, that is, in light of the sacramental presence of Christ’s sacrifice, that the text of the

Summa at III, q. 66, a. 9, ad 5, should be understood: “Christ’s death is commemorated in the sacrament of the Eucharist inasmuch as it is Christ who suffered [Christus passus] Himself is offered to us as a paschal banquet, as is said in 1 Cor 5: 7-8: ‘For our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast.’”292 Let us notice Saint Thomas’s expression, exhibetur nobis: He offers Himself to us, He presents Himself to us, He reveals Himself to us as a paschal banquet, under the form of food and drink, bread and wine, that is, under sacramental veils, under the separated species of bread and wine.

These considerations make it clear to us that the expression Christus passus is a true theological synthesis of many factors, not simply because it means that “Christ who has suffered” is contained in the Eucharist, but rather because it shows that the entirety of Christ’s Passion can be found in the Eucharist, and at the same time, it is not in a bloody way, since it is impossible that Christ risen from the dead can suffer.

Christus passus reveals that the reason for the form of the Sacrifice of the Mass is to be found in the mactatio mystica secundum se, in the unbloody immolation, that is, in the sacramental separation of Christ’s Blood from His Body, where Christ Immolated is shown and where He is placed “under sacramental species in the external vesture of death and destruction,”293 under “external signs which are the symbols of His death. . . . [By these] Jesus Christ is symbolically shown by separate symbols to be in a state of victimhood.” 294 This “in a state of victimhood” means that Christus passus could well be translated as Christ “passioned,”295 since “the Mass not only gives us Christ’s substantial presence in a glorious state, but also the operative presence of His sacrificial and redemptive act.”296 With this act, we also have the entirety of all the graces and merits He acquired on the cross and which are applied in the sacrament, in such a way that “this sacrament brings about in man the effect which Christ’s Passion wrought in the world.”297
