SACRIFICE AND GLORY

The Eucharist “is more properly the sacrament of Christ’s Body 298

than of His Divinity.”

SAINT THOMAS

1. The Faith of the Church

The Council of Trent teaches: “And this faith has ever been in the Church of God, that, immediately after the consecration, the veritable Body of our Lord, and His veritable Blood, together with His soul and divinity, are under the species of bread and wine; but the Body indeed under the species of bread, and the Blood under the species of wine, by the force of the words; but the body itself under the species of wine, and the blood under the species of bread, and the soul under both, by the force of that natural connexion and concomitancy whereby the parts of Christ our Lord, who has now risen from the dead, to die no more, are united together; and the divinity, furthermore, on account of the admirable hypostatical union thereof with His body and soul. Wherefore it is most true, that as much is contained under either species as under both; for Christ whole and entire is under the species of bread, and under any part whatsoever of that species; likewise the whole (Christ) is under the species of wine, and under the parts thereof.”299

By the sacrament’s power, that is, by the words of consecration or by the double change (transubstantiation), only Christ’s Body is found under the appearance of bread, and, separately, only Christ’s Blood is found under the appearance of wine.

This happens per se300 and directe.301 By itself and directly, the Eucharist does not contain:

a) Christ’s Blood under the species of bread; b) Christ’s Body under the species of wine; c) Christ’s soul; d) Christ’s divinity; e) the dimensive quantity proper to the Body nor that proper to the Blood (meaning the dimensions and accidents that accompany quantity, such as weight, volume, and the like); f) the qualities of His Body and Blood, such as form, figure, color, and so on; g) the passible or changeable qualities which would permit the Body and Blood to undergo changes; h) the accidents of action and passion: hence, the Body, where the transubstantiation of the bread ends per se, cannot receive actions that could come to it from an agent external to it. Christ’s Body cannot be seen, touched, chopped up, made to suffer, or murdered; i) Consequently, the different states of the Lord’s visible nature are not found directly or per se in the Eucharist. That is to say, neither His mortal and passible state, His Bloodless and soulless state, nor His immortal and glorious state are to be found there directly as a result of transubstantiation. Nonetheless, we still speak of Christ as being in a state of victimhood: Christ is a true victim, and He is found in that state. However, this happens not because He undergoes or suffers the action of some agent who causes Him pain or death itself; no, it happens for an entirely different reason: it happens as a result of the double consecration which places the substance of Christ’s Blood on the altar under one species separately from the substance of the Body.

2. The fundamental difference between vi sacramenti and vi concomitantiae

We must keep in mind what follows, because we are drawing near to the heart of the Eucharist as a sacrifice.

We will explain this with five arguments or distinctions:

a) Per se versus per accidens. Saint Thomas teaches: “The mode of existence for anything is determined by what pertains to that thing essentially, and not according to what is accidental to it. For example, if a body is seen, it is because it is white, and not because it is sweet, although the same body might be both white and sweet. Thus, sweetness would also be in sight, but according to the mode of whiteness, and not according to the mode of sweetness. It is by the sacrament’s power that the substance of Christ’s Body is on the altar; its dimensive quantity is there concomitantly and, as it were, accidentally [quasi per accidens] and not according to its proper mode, but rather after the manner of substance.”302

Thus it is clear that the way in which a thing exists, its mode of existing, is determined by what pertains to it essentially, and not by what comes to it accidentally. If we see a white candy, we see it because it’s white, and not because it’s sweet, although the white candy is sweet. Although sweetness is also in sight, it is in sight according to the mode proper to whiteness, and not according to the mode of sweetness. Analogously, then, by the sacrament’s power only the substance of Blood, separated from the Lord’s Body, with its sacrificial value, is present under the species of wine, and this pertains to the Eucharist essentially. Christ’s glorified Body is also present under the species of wine, but this only happens accidentally, as it were, since it happens by concomitance. In our Masses, celebrated after the Lord’s resurrection, Christ’s glorified Body is also present, but not according to the mode proper to His glorified Body, but rather according to the mode proper to the sacramental sacrifice.

b) Directe versus non fit per se. Now then, everything that comes in the Eucharist by concomitance is found indissolubly united to the Lord’s Body and Blood; however, with respect to the sacrament’s power, they are “per accidens,”303 that is, following the way in which accidents are found in a substance. They are present not directly but rather indirectly, in such a way that “the power of the sacramental words extends to making Christ’s Body [and Blood] present, whatever might be the accidents that really exist in it.” 304 Dom Vonier says that this “final phrase is a real stroke of genius.”305

c) This glorious aspect does not cancel or negate the

sacrificial reality. What is per accidens doesn’t divide a genus,306 and so, by means of analogy, what takes place in the sacrament quasi per accidens, that is, by concomitance, shouldn’t be considered as though it were some different genus with respect to what takes place in the sacrament per se and directe (by means of the sacramental change) through which the sacramental sacrifice is completely and directly carried out.

d) What is substantial doesn’t depend on what is

accidental, and vice versa. As we know, what is accidental depends more on the substance, that is, on what is essential, than the substance depends on what is accidental. 307 Analogously, then, we should think that whatever is present in the Eucharist per accidens depends more on what is there essentially than whatever is present essentially depends on what is there accidentally. Both take place at the same instant, but what is there by concomitance is only there if the Lord’s Body and Blood are there as well. Hence, Christ’s glorious state doesn’t prevent Christ from showing Himself in a state of victimhood; it is because of this victimal state that the Eucharist is directly and essentially a sacrifice.

When we use the phrase as it were accidentally, we mean a mode of being in which one thing is found in another, analogously to the way that accidents are found in a substance: they accompany it and are concomitant with it. However, with respect to the Eucharist we are not speaking of metaphysical accidents, because everything that we find under the species of bread following the Consecration and everything that is concomitant with the Lord’s Body could be, metaphysically speaking, an accident (like dimensive quantity), a substantial part (like Christ’s Body), an incomplete substance (like Christ’s soul), or a complete substance (like His divinity). All of these realities are accidently, as it were, under the species of bread after consecration.

e) Each thing is what it is principally, and all the rest

is simply united to it. Saint Thomas clarifies this; “It should be noted that we consider what things are by examining what we find as principal or most important in them, and all other aspects seem to adhere to what is principal; in a certain way, these aspects are assumed and used by what is principal according to its disposition. This is clearly seen not only in civil society, in which the princes seem to be the whole of the kingdom and make use of others as they dispose, as though these others were parts of their own bodies, but also in the natural unions of body and soul. Although man is naturally made up of both body and soul, it seems that what is principal is his soul, as it is to this that the body adheres and it is the soul that makes use of the body for fitting activity. Likewise, in the union of God with a creature, divinity is not dragged down by human nature, but rather human nature is assumed by God, not to be converted into God but rather to adhere to Him. In a certain sense, then, it is in this way that the body and soul assumed are the Body and Soul of God Himself, just as the different parts of the body assumed by a soul are, in a certain sense, members of the soul itself.” 308 We can analogously apply this doctrine to the Eucharist, in which the sacrifice is what is principal, and everything else adheres in it; what is principle makes use of all the others according to its own disposition.

3. Christ’s glorious state is not included directly, that is, per se, in the nature of the sacrament

As Pope Pius XII said, Jesus is present in the Eucharist “by external signs which are the symbols of His death,”309 as Blood separated from His Blood. Saint Peter Julian Eymard beautifully affirms this: “He puts on as much of death as He can; He is in a state of death; He is ‘a lamb as it were slain’ for us.”310 This is why Saint Thomas teaches that the Eucharist “is more properly the sacrament of Christ’s Body than of His Divinity,”311 and he beckons his readers to read further, where he examines the mode of presence of Christ’s soul and divinity in the Eucharist because of concomitance.312

Christ’s glorious state doesn’t enter per se in the nature of the sacrament; nor, for that matter, do Christ’s other states enter directly: “they do not enter directly into the nature of the sacrament as such: the sacrament transcends them. The sacrament is equal true, equally potent, equally direct . . . ”313 no matter the state Christ is in. Now-a-days, “almost the whole of Eucharistic literature, and a vast amount of the Eucharistic worship and devotion is based more on the concomitant elements of the Eucharist than on its sacramental elements,”314 so much so that often the Eucharist’s sacrificial reality is completely clouded over.

To deny the distinction between what is in the Eucharist ex vi sacramenti and what is there ex vi concomitantiae (although this might not be a distinction de fide) would be erroneous and rash, not only because of the Council of Trent’s authority, which used these expressions in order to explain the mystery, but also because this distinction is clearly derived from principles of the faith.315

4. The hypostatic union belongs to concomitance

Some theologians say that the possessive pronoun “my” in the consecration of the bread and the wine refers to the hypostatic union; thus, they say that Christ’s divinity would be found in the Eucharist ex vi sacramenti. However, this is not the case, since the words “This is my Body” mean only “Christ’s Body insofar as He is man and, thus, insofar as it is a human body; this is because neither the subsistence nor the hypostatic union are of its essence; nor are they one of its essential parts. Furthermore, Christ the Lord’s Body died and was given up insofar as it was human, even though it was truly united to the divinity. Thus, Christ’s divinity is meant or signified [in the words of the consecration] only secondarily and consequently.” 316 Christ’s divinity is present concomitantly, having never abandoned the Body that it assumed.317

Saint Thomas confirms this explicitly: “This pronoun of the first person, ‘my,’ points to the person who speaks, and thus sufficiently points to Christ’s person, in whose person these words are uttered.”318

5. The Body is never without the Blood, and vice versa

The case of concomitance that usually brings the most difficulties with it is this one: “The aspect of concomitance more directly concerned with the sacrifice of the Mass is this, that now the Body is never without the Blood, and the Blood is never without the Body in the Eucharistic sacrifice. For a good many people this dogmatic fact has obscured the fundamental notions of the Eucharistic sacrifice. They seem to be under the impression that, owing to the inseparability of Body and Blood, the Eucharist is not a drastic enough immolation, unless we look elsewhere for sacrificial features. . . . Do we not give God in the Eucharistic sacrifice the two things He loves best in this world, the Body and Blood of His Son? That such a Body and such Blood be wrapped up in every kind of glory; that they be even enfolded in each other, does certainly not interfere with the perfection of the gift, nor with the precise nature of the gift. There would be no sacrifice if the gift were something less than Body and Blood; but why should the presence of fresh glories in the Body and Blood interfere with the sacrifice? Provided we approach God carrying the Flesh and Blood of the Victim, in virtue of our sacramental ministry, we do a clearly-defined sacerdotal thing. That God should make our gift something fuller than does our ministry, how can this create confusion? In these high regions of divine life realities are inseparable; they accompany each other, without destroying each other’s individual identity.”319

What an incomparable burst from a passionate, priestly heart, giving an ad hominem argument of great value and strength on that plane! Nevertheless, we maintain that the scientific response to this difficulty is, again, this: a thing’s mode of existence is determined by what pertains to it essentially, and not by that which comes to it accidentally, as it were. When we see a white candy, we see it because it’s white, and not because it’s sweet, although the white candy is in fact sweet. Sweetness is also in sight, but according to the mode of being proper to whiteness, and not according to the mode of sweetness. Analogously, by the sacrament’s power only the substance of Blood, with its sacrificial value and separated from Lord’s Body, is present under the species of wine; this pertains to the Eucharist essentially. Christ’s Body is also with His Blood, though by concomitance, and His Blood is with His Body through concomitance, but this happens accidentally, as it were, precisely because it happens by concomitance. These are present by concomitance, and are therefore not present according to their proper mode of being, but rather according to the mode proper to the other sacramental reality (the one present ex vi sacramenti), that is, the Blood under the species of bread and the Body under that of wine: this occurs accidentally, as it were, and not per se.

It seems that Saint Thomas sees it this way. At least twice he shows the difference between the way the Body and the Blood are in the sacrament by the sacrament’s power itself and by concomitance.

1. When Saint Thomas raises the objection that what has already been done cannot be done again: “What has already happened cannot come to happen again. However, Christ’s Body already starts to be present in this sacrament with the consecration of the bread. Hence, it cannot come to present again with the consecration of the wine. Thus, Christ’s Body will not be contained under the species of wine, and consequently the whole Christ will not be contained there. Therefore, the whole Christ is not contained under each one of the species.” 320 He answers this objection saying: “As was said earlier, Christ’s Body is not under the species of wine by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti], but rather by real concomitance; hence, by the consecration the wine doesn’t contain Christ’s Body directly [per se], but rather only concomitantly.”321

2. When Saint Thomas raises the objection that, before the consecration of the wine, Christ’s Body would be without the Blood: “Just as with the consecration of the bread, Christ’s Body begins to be present under it, with the consecration of the wine, Christ’s Blood becomes present. If the words of consecration of the bread were to have their effect before the consecration of the wine, it would follow that in this sacrament Christ’s Body would be present without the Blood, which is not fitting.”322 The Angelic Doctor defeats this objection with the following logic: “Those who maintain this opinion seem to have erred, and for this reason: it must be understood that when the consecration of the bread is complete, Christ’s Body is there by the sacrament’s power [ex vi sacramenti], and the Blood present by real concomitance; after the consecration of the wine, however, Christ’s Blood is present by the sacrament’s power, and His Body by real concomitance. Hence the whole Christ is present under either species, as was said earlier.”323

As the Abbot Vonier says, “We must remember . . . that the sacrificial aspect of the Eucharist is saved only through our giving due prominence to what is in the Eucharist ex vi sacramenti. Dogmatically, too, this distinction is supremely vital for the defense of the ancient faith . . . . Let us remember that, while the whole Christ is in this sacrament—though not in virtue of the sacrament—He is there per modum sacramenti; not in a natural mode of being, but in an entirely new mode of being, the sacramental mode.”324 Saint Thomas also affirms that there are two ways of being for Christ’s Body: there is a mode of being secundum se, and another in the sacrament. One is the natural mode of being, and the other pertains to His sacramental presence: “Christ’s being in Himself and being in the sacrament are not the same, since when we say that

Christ is in this sacrament, we express a certain relationship with it.”325

This is indirectly confirmed by another argument that Saint Thomas gives, distinguishing between Christ’s humanity and His sacrament: “The greater the person whom one sins against, the greater the sin. Christ’s divinity is greater than His humanity, and His humanity is greater than the sacraments of His humanity. Therefore, the gravest sins are those committed against His divinity itself, such as unbelief and blasphemy. The second most grave sins are those committed against His humanity, and so we read in Saint Matthew’s Gospel: ‘And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come’ [Mt 12:32]. Thirdly, we have those sins which are committed against the sacraments, which belong to Christ’s humanity and, lastly, we have sins committed against creatures.”326

Returning to the distinction between sacrament and concomitance, Cardinal Billot affirmed: “This distinction, contained in the Council of Trent . . . is of great importance for understanding the whole of the mystery of the Eucharist. This is because, by affirming that ex vi sacramenti only the Lord’s Body is present under the species of bread, and only the Blood under the species of wine, the foundation is laid for the doctrine of the sacrifice of the Mass.”327

I have the impression that it is the forgetting of this explanation of the Eucharistic mystery, an explanation that establishes the foundations of the doctrine of the Mass as a sacrifice, that has led many priests to fall, perhaps unwillingly, into liturgical abuses and aberrations. It is these abuses that assail so many Christian men and women who, with serenity and simplicity, continue to fight the good fight of faith in the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass.

To cast this doctrine aside is to voluntarily make oneself incapable of being always ready to give an explanation to anyone who asks you for a reason for your hope (1 Pet 3:15). It means falling into a Eucharistic fideism that is unable to explain why the Mass is a sacrifice.

6. The Teaching of Pope Pius XII

We now recall what Pope Pius XII taught about the nature of the Eucharistic sacrifice in his encyclical Mediator Dei:

a) It is not a mere commemoration: “The august sacrifice of the altar, then, is no mere empty commemoration of the passion and death of Jesus Christ, but a true and proper act of sacrifice, whereby the High Priest by an unbloody immolation offers Himself a most acceptable victim to the Eternal Father, as He did upon the cross. ‘It is one and the same victim; the same person now offers it by the ministry of His priests, who then offered Himself on the cross, the manner of offering alone being different’ [Council of Trent, sess. 22, c. 2, Dz 940.]”

b) Comparison with the sacrifice of the Cross 1. The same priest: “The priest is the same, Jesus Christ, whose sacred Person His minister represents. Now the minister, on account of the sacerdotal consecration which he has received, is made like to the High Priest and possesses the power of performing actions in virtue of Christ’s very person [cfr. S. Th., III, q. 22, a. 4]. Wherefore in his priestly activity he in a certain manner ‘lends his tongue, and gives his hand’ to Christ [Saint John Chrysostom].”

2. The same victim: “Likewise the victim is the same, namely, our divine Redeemer in His human nature with His true body and blood.”

3. Different manner: “The manner, however, in which Christ is offered is different. On the cross He completely offered Himself and all His sufferings to God, and the immolation of the victim was brought about by the bloody death, which He underwent of His free will. But on the altar, because of the glorified state of His human nature, ‘death shall have no more dominion over Him’ [Rom 6:9], and so the shedding of His blood is impossible; still, according to the plan of divine wisdom, the sacrifice of our Redeemer is shown forth in an admirable manner by external signs which are the symbols of His death. For by the ‘transubstantiation’ of bread into the body of Christ and of wine into His blood, His body and blood are both really present: now the Eucharistic species under which He is present symbolize the actual separation of His body and blood.

Thus the commemorative representation of His death, which actually took place on Calvary, is repeated in every sacrifice of the altar, seeing that Jesus Christ is symbolically shown by separate symbols to be in a state of victimhood.”328 Christ’s death on the cross is always and inexorably signified and shown through the double consecration, in the carrying out of the matatio mystica.329 It is for this reason that the Mass is a sacrifice per se, and, moreover, it will always be a sacrifice, despite those who affirm the contrary.

328 Pius XII, Mediator Dei, 86-89: “Augustum igitur altaris Sacrificium non mera est ac simplex Iesu Christi cruciatuum ac mortis commemoratio, sed vera ac propria sacrificatio, qua quidem per incruentam immolationem Summus Sacerdos id agit, quod iam in Cruce fecit, semel ipsum aeterno Patri hostiam offerens acceptissimam. ‘Una . . . eademque est hostia, idem nunc offerens sacerdotum ministerio, qui se ipsum tunc in Cruce obtulit, sola offerendi ratione diversa’ [Conc. Trid. Sess. XXII, c. 1: Concilio Oecumenicorum Decreta, EDB,

This is why Pope Paul VI taught: “The sacramental signs of the Eucharist . . . contain Him, Christ, alive and real . . . but represented here in His sacrificial act.”330

7. The Victim’s Glory doesn’t void the sacrifice

The fact that now-a-days and by concomitance it is the resurrected Christ who is present doesn’t destroy or diminish the fact that the Eucharist sacramentally contains Christus passus. There is no contradiction, nor can there be contradiction, because these two are present under different aspects. 331 That the Eucharist sacramentally contains the Christus passus doesn’t interfere with the fact that by concomitance it is the risen Christ, glorious and immortal, who is there. I think that, just as the wounds of Christ’s glorious Body, far from diminishing the reality of the resurrection, extol it, since they speak to us of the great work of the sacrifice of the Cross, so, analogously, Christ’s Blood separated from His Body in the Eucharist, representing the Lord’s passion, does not for a moment diminish the dignity of the Risen lord, but rather exalts it, and vice versa.

This is why in the Mass we say: “We proclaim Your death, O Lord, and profess Your Resurrection.”

The Resurrection doesn’t render void the sacrifice that was its antechamber, nor does the sacrifice cancel out the Resurrection that was the sacrifice’s culmination.

In a splendid way, the Eucharist includes both of the great mysteries of our Lord’s Passover, like the two faces of one coin. It is the Paschal mystery of Jesus Christ’s death and resurrection!

Ignorance of this fundamental distinction, that is, of the two different modes of the Lord’s presence in the Eucharist, ex vi sacramenti and ex vi concomitantiae, a distinction sanctioned by the Council of Trent,332 leads to the darkening, distortion, forgetting, or even denial of the sacrificial reality of the Eucharist; this is because without this distinction, there is no way to reconcile the fact that Christ’s body given up (Lk 22:19; cfr. 1 Cor 11:24) and His shed blood (Mt 26:28, Mk 14:24, Lk 22:20) are truly present from the sacramental standpoint, and, yet, from the point of view of concomitance, Our Lord, glorious and immortal, is there. Dom Vonier said, “It is through that distinction between the virtue of the sacrament and concomitance that we are able to preserve the sacrificial aspect of the Eucharist.”333

We also see this importance of this distinction at the Synod of Bishops held regarding the Eucharist in 2005. In the Instrumentum laboris, we read that, in response to the Lineamenta, many of the participants had asked for a clarification of the Eucharist as sacrifice: “The Lineamenta responses indicate a general need to examine thoroughly the sacrificial nature of the Eucharist and a hope that this truth of our faith be presented with greater clarity, according to the recent Magisterium of the Church.”334

May we never forget that the Eucharist “is more properly the sacrament of Christ’s Body than of His Divinity.”335 This has been true for 2,000 years, and will remain so until the end of the world.

Saint Paul continues teaching us what he himself received from the Lord: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor 11:26).

8. Concorporeous, consanguineous, co-victims, co-offered, and co-accepted with Christ

Who has the leading role in the Holy Mass?

The most important role is held by the Second Person of the Most Holy Trinity: The Word, hypostatically united to the nature He assumed in the womb of the Virgin Mary, Jesus Christ, the Eternal High Priest. He is the lead actor at every Mass. He is its creator; He thought up the Mass for us. The One who prepared the table in the Cenacle is also the one who prepares the table upon our altars. He is the one who actually and principally offers each Mass, not by the multiplication of interior acts of oblation or offerings, but rather by a permanent act that endures in His soul. He solemnly commanded us to offer the Victim until the end of time: Do this in memory of Me.

The offertorial attitude of the Christian and of the priest should extend throughout the entire Eucharist, because it is an attitude that characterizes the entirety of Christian life and should, strictly speaking, also be extended to every part of it. However, we might ask ourselves: at which point in the Mass do we perceive this reality most concretely? At three different times:

1. In the preparation and presentation of the gifts; 2. In the Eucharistic prayer; 3. In Communion We will examine only the second moment. With respect to the Eucharist Prayer, we have two principal moments:

A. The Double Consecration

In the account of the institution of the Eucharist, as well as in the double consecration, the ministerial priest repeats these words in the name of Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Word: “This is My Body which will be given up. . . . This is the chalice of My Blood which will be poured out.”336 By reason of Christ’s words and the Holy Spirit’s power, the transubstantiation of the bread and the wine into the Lord’s Body and Blood is carried out in that moment. Through the double consecration, the Blood appears under the sacrament on one side, poured, and the Body on another, given up, which indicates that the sacrifice of the Cross is being perpetuated. The ministerial priest acts in Persona Christi. In this moment we have the Eucharistic immolation, the oblation or offering of the immolated Victim, and the Father’s acceptance of Him.

These elements are there so that we might be able to become Christ-bears by being “concorporeous, consanguineous,”337 co-victims (or co-sacrificed), co-offered, and co-accepted with Christ, that is, only one thing with Him.

Thus we are:

a) Concorporeous, becoming only one body with His Body when we unite ourselves to Him;

b) Consanguineous, by being only one thing with His Blood by being partakers of it. “In the Eucharist, the Church’s inner nature is revealed, a community of those summoned to the synaxis to celebrate the gift of the One who is offering and offered: participating in the Holy Mysteries, they become ‘kinsmen’338 of Christ, anticipating the experience of divinization in the now inseparable bond linking divinity and humanity in Christ.”339

c) Co-victims (or co-sacrificed), uniting ourselves with His Victimization and as victims to the Divine Victim.

d) Co-offered, becoming one thing with His Soul by His free will with which He offers His Sacrifice, and which is, at the same time, offered by us with Him, and our sacrifices together with His.

e) Co-accepted, by God the Father, who accepts the Sacrifice that is offered: He absolutely accepts that of His Son, and relatively (because He can reject it, according to our dispositions) accepts ours, the sacrifice of His Son’s children.

We also perceive the reality of the Eternal High Priest in the person of the ministerial priest, who is the sacramental figure of Jesus Christ, Head and Shepherd.

The words “This is My Body which will be given up. . . . This is the chalice of My Blood which will be poured out” indicate Christ’s Body and Blood are really made present under the appearances of bread and wine, the Body and Blood He offers as a bloody victim on Calvary and in unbloody form in the Mass. However, these words also imply His Mystical Body, as the Head is united to its members, forming only one mystical Person. Thus, He offers all the baptized as victims but, in a very special way, all of His ministerial priests.340

In that moment, we should unite ourselves to Christ, offering Him as the Victim of expiation for the sins of all men, joining our offering as victims to His, and the spiritual sacrifices of all of our brothers. Saint Thomas teaches: “Grace was in Christ not merely as in an individual, but also as in the Head of the whole Church, to Whom all are united, as members to a head, who constitute one mystical person.”341 He continues, saying: “Grace was bestowed upon Christ, not only as an individual, but inasmuch as He is the Head of the Church, so that it might overflow into His members; and therefore Christ’s works are referred to Himself and to His members in the same way as the works of any other man in a state of grace are referred to himself,” and he further insists, “For since He is our head, then, by the Passion which He endured from love and obedience, He delivered us as His members from our sins, as by the price of His Passion: in the same way as if a man by the good industry of his hands were to redeem himself from a sin committed with his feet. For, just as the natural body is one though made up of diverse members, so the whole Church, Christ’s mystical body, is reckoned as one person with its head, which is Christ.”342

This ineffable reality of the Christian’s incorporation into the Lord leads Saint Paul to create new expressions; even these new expressions, however, cannot completely express the mystery:

a) conmortui (2 Tim 2:11) meaning we have died with Him b) consepulti (Rom 6:4) meaning we were buried with him c) conresuscitati (Eph 2:6) meaning we were raised up with him d) convivificavit (Eph 2:5) meaning we were brought to life with Christ

e) complantati (Rom 6:5) meaning we have grown into union with Him

f) convivemus (2 Tim 2:11) meaning we shall also live with Him

g) consedere (Eph 2:6) meaning seated us with him in the heavens in Christ Jesus

We dare to continue this tradition, which seems also to include Saint Cyril of Jerusalem and other saints, in order to express, as best we can, our incorporation into Jesus Christ at the Holy Mass and throughout our lives, that is, to be

Christ-bearers (those who bring Christ) by being concorporeous, consanguineous, co-victims (or cosacrificed), co-offered, and co-accepted with Christ.

B. The Doxology

In the final doxology it is clear that Jesus Christ is the Eternal High Priest and the principal Priest of the Mass: “Through him, and with him, and in him, O God, almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, all glory and honor is yours, for ever and ever.” The congregation responds: “Amen.”343

“Through Him”: Christ is the Only Priest. He is the High Priest, the Eternal Priest, and the Principal Priest. He alone is the way to the Father. We must do everything by means of Christ, through Christ, by Christ. There is no salvation through anyone else (cfr. Acts 4:12). In way a similar to how the Christian faithful offer their spiritual sacrifices to the Father by means of the ministerial priest, the priest offers the sacrifices of the people, his own sacrifices as a victim, and the sacrifice of Jesus Christ by means of Him.

“With Him”: As Jesus Christ is the Only, High, Eternal, and Principal Priest, in addition to offering the sacrifices of the faithful, that of the ministerial priest as victim, and Jesus Christ’s sacrifice, we must offer these sacrifices by being intimately united to Him, together with Him, incorporated to Him. Just as the faithful offer their sacrifices to the Father together with the ministerial priest, in a similar way, the ministerial priest offers the Father the sacrifices together with the Son (although the sacrifice of the Only Son retains ontological priority).

“In Him”: Since we’re dealing with a Priest who has unique and unrepeatable characteristics, the sacrificial offering should be made within Him, identified with Him, in Him. We are a part of Christ, because we form the totality of Christ, that is, Christ plus us. We are another Christ, but here another Christ does not mean different from the true Christ, but rather that we must make ourselves one with the one and only Christ: “incorporating us to Himself, making us His members so that in Him we also might be Christ. . . . All of us in Him are of Christ and we are Christ, because, in a certain sense, the total Christ is head and body.”344 The ministerial priest should offer himself as a victim in Christ in a special way.

“Almighty Father”: the Sacrifice is offered to the Father and expresses His greatest glorification.

“In the unity of the Holy Spirit”: it is the glory of the Holy Trinity.

“All glory and honor is Yours, forever and ever”: the Trinity receives all of the glory and all of the honor. It is the supreme worship of latria or adoration, worship that is only rendered to the Supreme Being: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Amen”: the people affirm and confirm all of this.

Let us think, then, as John Paul II did: “Thus an essential aspect of the priestly life is illuminated: the priest is a man of sacrifice. In virtue of the sacrament of Orders, he has the mission of offering the sacrifice of Christ, making it mystically present in the reality of His Body and His Blood.

Thus, through his very priestly existence he is united to the redeeming sacrifice of Christ. Priestly ordination commits him to the path of this sacrifice. . . .

The priest knows that he is called to sacrifice in a particular way. Nevertheless, he will find the strength to generously endure his trials, in spite of difficulties, if he knows how to see them in the light of Christ’s passion. Did not Saint Paul say Now I rejoice in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am filling up what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ on behalf of his body, which is the church (Col 1:24)?”345

May the Mother of Priests help us to be faithful to Her Son.

The lead actor is always the Word made flesh!

UNITY

“The safeguarding and promotion of ecclesial communion is a task of

each member of the faithful, who finds in the Eucharist, as the 346 sacrament of the Church’s unity, an area of special concern.”

POPE JOHN PAUL II

The Eucharist both signifies and causes the Church’s unity. The second effect of the sacrament-sacrifice, the res tantum, is that ineffable reality of unity.

“From what the Apostle says, ‘Because the loaf of bread is one, we, though many, are one body, for we all partake of the one loaf,’ [1 Cor 10:17] it is clear that the Eucharist is the sacrament of the Church’s unity.”347

“Its effect [res tantum] is the unity of the mystical body, without which there can be no salvation, since there is no entering into salvation apart from the Church, just as in the time of the flood there was no salvation outside of Noah’s ark, which is a symbol of the church, as Peter says [1 Pet 3:20-21]. As said above, a sacrament’s effect can be had even before receiving it through the very desire to receive it. Hence, a person can be saved before the reception of this sacrament through their desire for it, just as one can be saved before baptism through the desire for it.”348 “As Augustine says when explaining John’s words, ‘this food and drink,’ that is, His Body and His Blood: ‘Christ wants us to understand this as the communion of His body and members, which is the Church in the predestined, called, justified, in His glorified saints and in believers.’ Thus, as he himself says in his letter to Boniface, ‘There is no doubt that the faithful are made participants in the Lord’s Body and Blood when they are made members of Christ’s Body at baptism. They are not deprived of their share of that bread and that wine, even if they were not to eat or drink of it, if they leave this world constituted in the unity of that Body.’”349 “Baptism is the sacrament of Christ’s passion and death inasmuch as man is born anew in Christ by the power of His passion. In contrast, the Eucharist is the sacrament of Christ’s Passion insofar as man is made perfect in union with Christ who suffered. Just as baptism is called the ‘sacrament of faith,’ which is the foundation of the spiritual life, the Eucharist is called ‘the sacrament of charity’ which is ‘the bond of perfection,’ as the Apostle says.”350 “This sacrament has a three-fold meaning. . . . The second meaning that it has with respect to the present is that of ecclesiastical unity, into which people are gathered by this sacrament. This is why it is called ‘communion,’ or ‘synaxis.’ Thus, as Damascene says, ‘It is called communion because through it we communicate with Christ, partaking of His flesh and His divinity, and because we communicate and are mutually united with each other.’”351

Saint Thomas raises an interesting objection: “Men are united to Christ as members to their head by means of this sacrament. However, Christ is the head of all men, even those who have existed since the world began. Thus, the institution of the Eucharist should not have been delayed until the Last Supper.” He responds in this way: “The Eucharist is the perfect sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, in as much as it contains Christ Himself who has suffered [Christum passum]; thus it could not be instituted before the Incarnation, and so there was only a place for sacraments [of the Old Testament] that were a prefiguration of the Lord’s Passion.”352

It was fitting that Our Lord use bread and wine as the matter for the unbloody sacrifice because of “the effect on the whole Church, which is made up of many faithful; ‘just as bread is made from many grains, and wine flows from many grapes,’ as the gloss says on 1 Cor 10:17: ‘We, though many, are one body.’”353 “Even though the flesh of dead animals more prominently represents Christ’s passion, it is less suitable for common use of the sacrament and for signifying the Church’s unity.”354

The adding of some drops of water to the wine in the offertory helps with this representation, “because this is in accord with effect of this sacrament, which is the union of the Christian people with Christ; hence, as Pope Julius said, ‘In the water, we understand the people, but, by the wine, we are shown Christ’s Blood. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are made one with Christ.”355

This sacrament’s effect is revealed by the species in which it comes about: “This sacrament’s effect can be considered from the species under which it is given. As Augustine says ‘Our Lord gave His Body and Blood in things that are made from many into one: namely, bread ‘for from many grains, one thing is made,’ and wine, ‘for it flows from many clusters.’ Elsewhere he says, ‘O sacrament of piety, o sign of unity, o bond of charity!’ Since Christ and His passion are the cause of grace, and there is neither spiritual refreshment nor charity without grace, it is clear that this sacrament confers grace.”356

Hence: “this sacrament spiritually confers grace along with the virtue of charity. Damascene compares this sacrament to the burning coal that Isaiah saw: ‘as the ember is not simply wood, but wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple, but rather united to the divinity.’ However, as Gregory says . . . ‘God’s love is not idle, but rather does great works wherever it is present,’ and hence it follows that this sacrament not only has the power to give the habit of grace and virtue, but also to move to act, because ‘the love of Christ impels us’ [2 Cor 5:14].”357

In this life, unity and peace are obtained only imperfectly, but it will not be this way in glory: “The refreshment of spiritual food, and the unity signified by the species of bread and wine, are had in this present life, albeit imperfectly; these will be perfectly had, however, in the state of glory. Thus Augustine, commenting on the words ‘My flesh is true food,’ says, ‘In eating and drinking, men desire to hunger and thirst no more, and only this food and this drink [of the Eucharist] so satisfy man, the food and drink by which men are made incorruptible and immortal in the communion of the saints, where perfect and full peace and unity are.’”358 “As a sacrament, the Eucharist produces its effect in two ways: the first directly by the sacrament’s power, and the second by a certain concomitance. . . . This distinction is also used when speaking about the ways in which Christ is contained in the sacrament. Now, by the sacrament’s power, it directly produces the effect for which it was instituted. The Eucharist was not instituted for the satisfaction of sins, but rather to spiritually nurture us by means of union with Christ and with His members, just as food is united to the one who is nourished. However, this union comes about by means of charity, from the fervor of which man obtains not only the remission of his guilt, but also of the punishment due him. Hence, it is as a consequence, by concomitance with the principal effect, that man obtains the remission of his punishment, though not of the entire punishment simply, but rather according to the measure of his devotion and fervor.

Inasmuch as it is a sacrifice, however, the Eucharist has a satisfactory power. In this satisfaction, though, the goodwill of the offerer is considered more than the quantity of the offering (as the Lord says of the widow who gave two small coins, she ‘put in more than all the rest’). Hence, although this offering is in itself sufficient to satisfy for all punishment, it only satisfies for those for whom it is offered or for those who offer it, according to the measure of devotion that they have, and not for the whole punishment.”359 “Just as in the other sacraments, this sacrament is a sign of the effect that it produces. The effect [res] of this sacrament is two-fold, as we said earlier: one, which is signified and contained, which is Christ Himself, and another, signified yet not contained, which is the Mystical Body, the communion of the saints. Thus, whoever receives this sacrament, simply by the very fact of receiving it, expresses that he is united to Christ and incorporated in His members. This is done by living faith [informed faith, i.e., faith informed by charity], which no one in mortal sin has. It is evident, therefore, that whoever receives this sacrament while in a state of mortal sin lies to the sacrament, incurring the guilt of sacrilege, and thus sins mortally.”360

359 S. Th., III, q. 79, a. 5, corpus: “Si igitur consideretur ut sacramentum, habet dupliciter effectum, uno modo, directe ex vi sacramenti; alio modo, quasi “When Christ lived among us, in His own, proper, species, He did not give Himself to be touched by men as a sign of spiritual union with Himself, unlike what happens in this sacrament when it is received. Thus, sinners who touched Him while He lived among us did not incur the guilt of lying to God, unlike those sinners [in mortal sin] who receive this sacrament.

Moreover, Christ still bore ‘the likeness of sinful flesh,’ and this is why He let Himself be touched by sinners. However, as soon as that likeness of sinful flesh was left behind by the glory of the Resurrection, He forbid the woman whose faith was weak to touch Him, as we read: ‘Stop holding on to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father’ [Jn 20:17], that is, ‘in your heart,’ as Augustine explains. It is for this reason that sinners, who lack an informed faith in Christ [i.e., faith informed by charity], are not allowed to touch this sacrament.”361

Thus, with respect to those separated from the Catholic faith: “The impediment that goes against charity itself is weightier than one that goes against its fervor. This is why the sin of unbelief, which fundamentally separates a man from unity with the Church, is the sin that, simply speaking, renders him the most unfit to receive the Eucharist, as this sacrament is the sacrament of the Church’s unity, as said earlier. This is why the unbeliever who receives the sacrament sins more grievously than the believer who receives in a state of sin; the former despises Christ more in this sacrament, especially if he does not even believe that Christ is present in the sacrament, since, with respect to himself, he lessens the sacrament’s holiness and Christ’s power that acts in it, which is to despise the sacrament itself. However, the believer who receives while aware of grave sin and thus receives unworthily, despises the sacrament not in itself, but rather in its use. Referring to such sinners, the Apostle says, ‘without discerning the body,’ [1 Cor 11:29] meaning, ‘not distinguishing it from any other sort of food.’ This is precisely what the one who does not believe that Christ is present in the Eucharist does.”362

Here, it is absolutely necessary to mention Pope John Paul II’s encyclical letter, Ecclesia de Eucharistia, and to cite it, even if it’s no more than a few paragraphs: “The celebration of the Eucharist, however, cannot be the starting-point for communion; it presupposes that communion already exists, a communion which it seeks to consolidate and bring to perfection. The sacrament is an expression of this bond of communion both in its invisible dimension, which, in Christ and through the working of the Holy Spirit, unites us to the Father and among ourselves, and in its visible dimension, which entails communion in the teaching of the Apostles, in the sacraments and in the Church’s hierarchical order. The profound relationship between the invisible and the visible elements of ecclesial communion is constitutive of the Church as the sacrament of salvation [Cfr. Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Communionis notio, 4: AAS 85; 1993, 839-840]. Only in this context can there be a legitimate celebration of the Eucharist and true participation in it. Consequently it is an intrinsic requirement of the Eucharist that it should be celebrated in communion, and specifically maintaining the various bonds of that communion intact. . . .

The ecclesial communion of the Eucharistic assembly is a communion with its own Bishop and with the Roman Pontiff. The Bishop, in effect, is the visible principle and the foundation of unity within his particular Church [Lumen Gentium, 23]. It would therefore be a great contradiction if the sacrament par excellence of the Church’s unity were celebrated without true communion with the Bishop. As Saint Ignatius of Antioch wrote: ‘That Eucharist which is celebrated under the Bishop, or under one to whom the Bishop has given this charge, may be considered certain’ [PG 5, 713]. Likewise, since ‘the Roman Pontiff, as the successor of Peter, is the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity of the Bishops and of the multitude of the faithful,’ [Lumen Gentium, 23] communion with him is intrinsically required for the celebration of the Eucharistic Sacrifice. Hence the great truth expressed which the Liturgy expresses in a variety of ways: ‘Every celebration of the Eucharist is performed in union not only with the proper Bishop, but also with the Pope, with the episcopal order, with all the clergy, and with the entire people. Every valid celebration of the Eucharist expresses this universal communion with Peter and with the whole Church, or objectively calls for it, as in the case of the Christian Churches separated from Rome’ [Cfr.

Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Communionis notio, 14: AAS 85; 1993, 847].

The Eucharist creates communion and fosters communion. Saint Paul wrote to the faithful of Corinth explaining how their divisions, reflected in their Eucharistic gatherings, contradicted what they were celebrating, the Lord’s Supper. The Apostle then urged them to reflect on the true reality of the Eucharist in order to return to the spirit of fraternal communion [Cfr. 1 Cor 11:17-34]. Saint Augustine effectively echoed this call when, in recalling the Apostle’s words: ‘You are the body of Christ and individually members of it’ [1 Cor 12:27], he went on to say: ‘If you are his body and members of him, then you will find set on the Lord's table your own mystery. Yes, you receive your own mystery’ [Sermon 272: PL 38, 1247]. And from this observation he concludes: “Christ the Lord . . . hallowed at his table the mystery of our peace and unity. Whoever receives the mystery of unity without preserving the bonds of peace receives not a mystery for his benefit but evidence against himself’ [Ibid., 1248].”363

We also have some beautiful texts from Saint Thomas: “The Eucharist is the sacrament of ecclesiastical unity, which comes about since many are ‘one in Christ Jesus.’”364

“By the power of the Holy Spirit, who by unity in charity communicates the mutual goods of Christ’s members, the private good of the Mass of a good priest is fruitful and beneficial to others as well. However, the private evil of one man cannot hurt another unless this latter consent to it in some way, as Augustine says,”365 because “the evil of the ministers cannot redound to the mysteries of Christ.”366 “Christ’s true Body is a figure of His mystical body. . . . The unity of the mystical body is the fruit of communion of the true Body. Those who receive or administer it unworthily are deprived of this unity.”367 “The people are prepared by the peace, which is given with the words ‘Lamb of God,’ since this is the sacrament of unity and peace.”368 “The Eucharist is the sacrament of the unity of the entire Church; hence in this sacrament, more than any other, mention should be made of all that pertains to the wellbeing of the entire Church.”369

The Mass is the triumphant hymn of the one Church: “The Church is called during her earthly pilgrimage to maintain and promote communion with the Triune God and communion among the faithful. For this purpose she possesses the word and the sacraments, particularly the Eucharist, by which she ‘constantly lives and grows’ [Lumen Gentium, 26] and in which she expresses her very nature. It is not by chance that the term communion has become one of the names given to this sublime sacrament.

The Eucharist thus appears as the culmination of all the sacraments in perfecting our communion with God the Father by identification with his only-begotten Son through the working of the Holy Spirit. With discerning faith a distinguished writer of the Byzantine tradition voiced this truth: in the Eucharist ‘unlike any other sacrament, the mystery [of communion] is so perfect that it brings us to the heights of every good thing: here is the ultimate goal of every human desire, because here we attain God and God joins himself to us in the most perfect union’ [N. Cabasilas, Life in Christ, IV, 10: SCh 355, 270]. Precisely for this reason it is good to cultivate in our hearts a constant desire for the sacrament of the Eucharist. This was the origin of the practice of ‘spiritual communion,’ which has happily been established in the Church for centuries and recommended by saints who were masters of the spiritual life. Saint Teresa of Jesus wrote: ‘When you do not receive communion and you do not attend Mass, you can make a spiritual communion, which is a most beneficial practice; by it the love of God will be greatly impressed on you’ [Camino de perfección, c. 35, 1].”370

GOD

“Before the preface, the priest prepares the souls of his brethren, saying ‘Lift up your hearts,’ so that the people might respond, ‘We lift them up to the Lord,’ and that they might know that they should think of 371

nothing other than God.”

SAINT CYPRIAN

1. God - Spirit

Everything that has been said about the sacraments comes from God’s revelation to man. It is something that is above, before, and beyond man. Hence, sacramental theology depends on God’s will and on the concrete commands that He has wanted to give regarding it. He set the signs that should be used, and, in the New Law, He made it so that the sacraments would not be mere signs, but also efficient causes. They signify grace because they give grace.

God has given us the sacraments for the perfection of our human nature, made with the dignity of being the “image and likeness” of God (cfr. Gen 1:26), as His sons and daughters, and as heirs to eternity. Since God doesn’t usually act with punches and kicks, but rather adjusts Himself to our nature (the Greek synkatabasis), as Scripture says, “[He] governs all things well,” He also, as we have seen, makes the spiritual life (as carried out through the sacraments) parallel natural life: there are sacraments for birth, growth, nutrition, cleaning, and so on.

The truth of the sacramental order is found in God, since this order is of divine institution; we know this by God’s explicit revelation. Thus, the ultimate basis and foundation for this order is the divine determination, which is definitive though not arbitrary; the sacraments are arranged fittingly. God wanted the sacraments to be as they were, as they are, and as they will be.

Also, He wanted them to be as they have come down to us, including their different families of rites (Antiochian- Byzantine,372 Roman, Coptic, and so on), which have their origins in the three primal sees of the Church, according to canon VI of the Council of Nicea,373 and that are linked with the traditions that come from Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles and the first Pope.374

In short, the Eucharist is a reality that comes from God and leads to God.

A. God

The Eucharist makes us participate in God’s life: “The second meaning that it has with respect to the present is that of ecclesiastical unity, into which people are gathered by this sacrament. This is why it is called ‘communion,’ or ‘synaxis.’ Thus, as Damascene says, ‘It is called communion because through it we communicate with Christ, partaking of His flesh and His divinity, and because we communicate and are mutually united with each other.”375 “In Greek, [the Eucharist] is called ‘metalepsis,’ which means ‘assumption,’ because, as Damascene says, ‘by it we assume the Son’s divinity.’”376

The Eucharist obtains salvation for us since it is propitiation before God by faith in Christ’s blood: “No one can be saved without faith in Christ’s passion: ‘whom God set forth as an expiation, through faith, by his blood.’ [Rom 3:25] So it was fitting that at all times men might have some representation of the Lord’s Passion. In the Old Testament, the special sacrament was the paschal lamb, and so the Apostle writes, in 1 Cor 5 [7], ‘Our paschal lamb, Christ, has been sacrificed.’ In the New Testament, the Eucharist succeeds the lamb, because, as the lamb was a figure of the future, the Eucharist is a remembrance of the past passion. So, it was fitting that, as His Passion was imminent and the old sacrament had been celebrated, Christ would institute the new sacrament, as Pope Leo says.” 377 The sacrifice of the New Testament must be propitiatory because we, the men and women for whom it was carried out, are sinners. “Inasmuch as it is a sacrifice the Eucharist has a satisfactory power.”378

The truth that the Son is really and truly God teaches us that our Lord’s Body and Blood are truly present in the Eucharist: “Saint Ambrose says ‘As the Lord Jesus Christ is truly God’s Son, so too is it Christ’s true Flesh that we consume, and His true Blood that we drink.’”379

It is impossible for a mere creature to transubstantiate: “The power of a finite agent cannot change one form into another, nor one material into another. However, the power of an infinite agent can make such a change, because its action reaches all being, and the nature of being is common to all forms and all matter. The author of being can convert what there is of being into something different, removing that by which they were distinguished from each other.”380

The Eucharist is the New Testament which must be sealed with blood: “A testament or will is the arrangement of an inheritance. God arranged the heavenly inheritance for man by the power of Christ’s blood, since ‘where there is a will, the death of the testator must be established’ [Heb 9:16]. Now, Christ’s blood has been given to men in two ways. The first was as a figure, which pertains to the Old Testament. Thus the Apostle concludes: ‘Thus not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood’ [Heb 9:18], as is clear from what was said in Exodus: Taking the book of the covenant, he read it aloud to the people, who answered, ‘All that the Lord has said, we will hear and do.’ Then he took the blood and splashed it on the people, saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you according to all these words’ [Ex 24: 7-8].

The second was in truth, which pertains to the New Testament. This is why the Apostle, a little earlier, says, ‘For this reason he is mediator of a new covenant: since a death has taken place for deliverance from transgressions under the first covenant, those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance’ [Heb 9:15]. Hence [in the form of consecration] we say, ‘blood of the new and eternal covenant,’ since it is no longer a mere figure, but the true reality that is produced. Hence, ‘which will be poured out for you,’ is also added. The internal inspiration [of the New Law] comes from the power of the blood since it is by Christ’s passion that we are justified.”381

The covenant with God that is renewed at every Mass is not only new, but also eternal, because this is the way that God arranged it, since our inheritance is eternal and since Christ’s Blood is united to the person of the Word, who is eternal: “This Testament is new on account of its appearance or showing forth. It is eternal, however, both because of God’s eternal ordaining, as well as the eternal inheritance which is prepared by it. Furthermore, the very person of Christ, whose Blood prepared this testament, is eternal.”382 “Saint Cyril says ‘By uniting Himself with His own flesh, the Life-giving Word of God made it life-giving as well. It was fitting that He would unite Himself to our bodies through His Sacred Flesh and His Precious Blood, which we receive in a life-giving blessing in the bread and wine.’”383

B. Spirit

Now-a-days, it’s fairly common to find people who classify Saint Thomas as a ‘static’ or ‘fixed’ philosopher, saying that he doesn’t mention the Holy Spirit’s action, or talk about the spirit in general. We know that this is really because these people consider themselves as ‘dynamic’ and ‘docile’ to the spirit: with regard to both, these people are in error.

In the Treatise on the Eucharist, Saint Thomas first speaks about the Holy Spirit in the very first question, in the very first article,: “The water of Baptism does not cause any spiritual effect because it is water, but rather on account of the power of the Holy Spirit that exists in the water. For this reason Chrysostom says, commenting on the Gospel of Saint John [5:4] For [from time to time] an angel of the Lord used to come down into the pool; and the water was stirred up, etc.: ‘The water alone does not act upon the baptized, but rather, when it receives the Holy Spirit’s grace, it then loosens all sins.’ The relation of the Holy Spirit’s power to the water of Baptism is the same as the relation of Christ’s true Body to the species of bread and wine. Thus, the species of bread and wine have no effect except from the power of Christ’s true Body.”384

“When Augustine says, ‘You will not eat this body that you see,’ he doesn’t mean to reject the truth of [the presence of] Christ’s body, but rather that it was not to be eaten in the species by which it is seen. In what he adds, ‘the sacrament that I commended to you will enliven your minds spiritually,’ he doesn’t mean that Christ’s body is in this sacrament merely according to some mystical meaning, but rather he says ‘spiritually’ meaning invisibly and by the Spirit’s power. Thus, when making an exposition on the words, ‘the flesh is of no avail,’ he says: ‘that is, in the way they understood it. They understood that they should eat the flesh as that which is cut from a cadaver or as that which is sold in the market, and not as though enlivened by the spirit. When the spirit comes to the flesh, it benefits greatly, for if the flesh were entirely of no avail, the Word would not have become flesh and dwelt among us.’ ”385 “These words of Augustine, and others like them, are to be understood of Christ’s body as it is seen in its proper species, according to what the Lord Himself said, ‘You will not always have me.’ However, He is invisibly present under the species of this sacrament wherever this sacrament is consecrated.”386 “This argument concerns the presence of Christ’s Body as it is present as a body, that is, as it is present in its visible species, and not, therefore, as it is spiritually, that is, invisibly, present, after the manner and power of a spirit. Thus Augustine says, ‘If you have understood Christ’s words about His flesh spiritually, then those words will be spirit and life to you; however, if you have understood them according to the flesh, those words will still be spirit and life, but not to you.’ ”387

Only the Holy Spirit’s power changes the bread and wine: “Damascene says, in Book IV, ‘The change of bread into Christ’s Body is done only by the Holy Spirit’s power.’”388

In the confection of the Eucharist, the Holy Spirit acts ex opera operato: “Augustine says, ‘In the Catholic Church, with respect to the mystery of the Lord’s Body and Blood, the good priest does not do more, nor the bad priest less, since the priest does not consecrate by virtue of his own merits, but rather by the Creator’s word and the Holy Spirit’s power.”389

When the question arises as to whether a sinful priest can celebrate the Eucharist, Saint Thomas cites Saint John Damascene and Pope Gelasius: “Damascene says that ‘by the coming of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine are supernaturally converted into the Lord’s Body and Blood.’ However, Pope Gelasius asks, ‘How can the Holy Spirit, invoked for the divine mystery of consecration, come, when it can be attested that the priest who entreats Him is full of evil deeds?’ Hence, an evil priest cannot consecrate the Eucharist. . . . To the second objection, I respond with the words of Pope Gelasius before those cited above: ‘This most holy rite, which contains the Catholic discipline, claims such reverence for itself that no one except those who are pure in conscience may dare to approach it.’ From these words, it is clear that the Pope’s intended meaning was that the sinful priest should not approach this sacrament. Hence, when he continues adding, ‘How can the Holy Spirit, invoked . . . come,’ it should be understood that the Spirit does not come through the priest’s merits, but rather through Christ’s power, whose words the priest offers.”390 “Gregory says, ‘Alas, into what a great snare they fall who believe that the divine and hidden mysteries offered by some are better than others, when it is one and the same Holy Spirit who, in a hidden and invisible way, acts to sanctify them!’ These hidden mysteries are celebrated in the Mass.’”391 “By the Holy Spirit’s power, who by unity in charity communicates the mutual goods of Christ’s members, the private good of the Mass of a good priest is fruitful and beneficial to others as well. However, the private evil of one man cannot hurt another unless this latter consent to it in some way, as Augustine says.”392

390 S. Th., III, q. 82, a. 5, obj. 2 et ad 2: “Damascenus dicit, in IV libro [De fide Orth., c. 13: PG 94,1145], quod ‘panis et vinum, per adventum Sancti Spiritus,

2. God acts by His power

God acts by His divine power in the change of the substance of bread and wine into the Lord’s Body and Blood: “Damascene says, ‘Since it is normal for men to consume bread and wine, God wedded His divinity to them, and made them His Body and Blood.’ Later he adds, ‘The bread of communion is not simply bread, but is, rather, united to His divinity.’” “God ‘married His divinity,’ that is, His divine power, to the bread and wine, not in order for these to remain in the sacrament, but rather that they might become His Body and His Blood.”393

“Augustine says, ‘God is not a cause that reduces being to non-being.’ However, this sacrament comes about by the divine power. Hence, in this sacrament, the substance of bread and wine are not annihilated.”394

Here, God works a supernatural change: “This change is not like other natural changes, but is, rather, completely supernatural, done only by God’s power.”395

The change carried out in each and every Eucharist is completely extraordinary; in each and every case, it is carried out by God’s infinite power: “It is clear that every agent acts insofar as it is in act. However, every created agent is finite in its act, just as it is in a determined genus and species. Thus, the action of every created agent is also limited to some determined act. The limitation of any one thing in its action comes from its form, and hence no natural or created agent can do anything beyond changing forms; for this reason, every change made according to the laws of nature is a formal change. However, God is infinite act, as was seen in the first part [q. 7, a. 2; q. 25, a. 2] and so His power extends to the entire nature of being. Thus God can cause not only formal changes, so that different forms follow each other in the same subject, but also the change of an entire being, so that the entire substance of one being is completely changed into the substance of another; this is what comes about by divine power in this sacrament.”396 “This change is done by an infinite power, to which it pertains to act instantaneously. . . . There are three reasons why this change is instantaneous. First, the substance of Christ’s Body, which is the end of this change, does not admit of a more or less. Secondly, in this change there is no subject that needs to be prepared gradually or successively. Thirdly, this change comes about by God’s infinite power. ”397 “This change does not occur by the passive potency of a creature, but rather only by the Creator’s active power.”398 “Christ’s Body does not remain in this sacrament only until the next day, but rather for an indeterminate amount of time; it remains as long as the sacramental species remain. When these species cease to be, Christ’s Body ceases to be under them, not because it depends on them, but rather because the relation that Christ’s Body has with those species is taken away, just as God stops being the Lord of creatures who have ceased to be.”399 “In this sacrament, the consecration of the matter consists of a miraculous change of substance, which only God can bring about.”400

In this sacrament, God acts:

efficiently and sacramentally, that is, by signification: “God’s word, which acted in the creation of all things, also acts in the consecration, though in a different manner. In the consecration, it acts sacramentally, that is, in virtue of what it signifies. Hence, it is fitting that the consecration’s last and ultimate effect be signified in this sentence by a substantive verb in the indicative mode and present tense. However, in the creation of things God’s word only acted efficiently, and this efficiency is on account of the command of His wisdom. This is why in creation God’s word is expressed by a verb in the imperative: ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light [Gen 1:3].’”401 by sustaining accidents without their proper subject: “It must be granted that the accidents in this sacrament remain without a subject, something that can be done by God’s power. This is because effects depend more on the first cause than on secondary causes and hence God, who is the first cause of both substance and accidents, can, by His infinite power, preserve accidents in being when their substantial subject is removed. These accidents maintain in being as by their proper cause, just as God can produce other natural effects without the natural causes, just as He formed a human body in the Virgin’s womb ‘without man’s seed.’ ”402 in allowing the accidents to act without a substantial form: “The action of an accidental form depends on the action of the substantial form, just as accidental being depends on substantial being. Hence, just as Divine power allows the sacramental species to exist without a substance, so also it is an effect of Divine power that the accidents can act without a substantial form, since the action of every form, substantial and accidental, depends on God as first agent.”403 without the accidents ceasing to be accidents: “Since being is not a genus, it can be the essence of neither substance nor accident. Thus, the definition of substance is not ‘a subsistent being without a subject’ [ens per se sine subiecto], nor that of accident ‘being in a subject’ [ens in subiecto]; rather, the quiddity or essence of a substance is ‘that to which it belongs to not have being in a subject,’ and that of accident ‘that to which it belongs to have being in a subject.’ Hence, in this sacrament, the accidents are not found without a subject by the power of their own essence, but rather by the Divine power that sustains them. Hence, they do not cease to be accidents, since they do not cease to meet the definition of accidents, nor do they meet the definition of substance.”404 “The accidents acquired their individual being in the substance of bread and wine. When these are converted into Christ’s Body and Blood, it is by the Divine power that the accidents retain the individual being that they had; hence they continue being singular and sensible.”405 “Lightness and heaviness are qualities derived from bodies on account of having little or much matter in their dimensions, and all other accidents are derived from the principles of substance. Hence it follows that, just as Divine power conserves all the other accidents in being when the substance is taken away, so too, when matter is removed, Divine power holds in being those qualities which follow on matter, such as lightness and heaviness.”406

The Principal Agent’s power acts through other, participated powers that He uses: “The sacramental power consists in several things, and not just one, just as Baptism’s power consists both in words and in water. Thus, the power for consecration consists not only in the words, but also in the power handed on to the priest in his consecration or ordination when the bishop says to him, ‘Receive the power of offering up the Sacrifice in the Church for the living as well as for the dead.’ Hence, the instrumental power is found in many instruments through which the principal agent acts.”407

God acts in the Eucharist, and the Eucharist unites us to God: “In itself, this sacrament has the power to confer grace, so much so that no one possesses grace before receiving it, at least in desire, be it of his own desire, as in the case of adults, or the Church’s desire, in the case of children, as was already said. The efficacy of the Eucharist’s power is such that just from desiring it man receives some grace by which he is given spiritual life. Nonetheless, when the sacrament itself is actually received, the grace is increased and spiritual life perfected. This is done in a manner different from the way done in the sacrament of Confirmation, in which grace is increased and perfected in order to resist the outward assaults of Christ’s enemies. However, in the Eucharist grace increases and the spiritual life perfected so that man might be perfect in himself by being joined to God.”408 “This sacrament spiritually confers grace along with the virtue of charity. Damascene compares this sacrament to the burning coal that Isaiah saw: ‘as the ember is not simply wood, but wood united to fire, so the bread of communion is not simple, but rather united to the divinity.’ However, as Gregory says . . . ‘God’s love is not idle, but rather does great works wherever it is present,’ and hence it follows that this sacrament not only has the power to give the habit of grace and virtue, but also to move to act, because ‘the love of Christ impels us’ [2 Cor 5:14]. Hence, it is by the sacrament’s power that the soul is nourished; by it the soul is delighted and inebriated, as it were, by the sweetness of the Divine goodness, as is read: ‘Eat, friends; drink! Drink deeply, lovers!’ [Sg 5:1].”409

Every Mass is offered to God “inasmuch as Christ’s passion is represented in this sacrament; His passion, in which ‘Christ loved us and handed himself over for us as a sacrificial offering to God for a fragrant aroma’ [Eph 5:2], has the nature of a sacrifice.”410

On account of their Baptism, the Christian lay faithful are capable of offering spiritual sacrifices to God: “The just lay person is united to Christ with a spiritual union by means of faith and charity, and not by means of sacramental power [that is, of Holy Orders]. Thus, the lay person possesses a spiritual priesthood for offering spiritual sacrifices, as the Psalm says, ‘My sacrifice, O God, is a contrite spirit’ [51:19], or as the Apostle comments, ‘Offer your bodies as a living sacrifice.’ This is why Peter speaks of ‘a holy priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ’ [1 Pet 2:5].”411

To consecrate and offer the Eucharist pertains to the ministerial priests: “The consecration of Christ’s Body pertains to the priest for . . . as was said above, he consecrates in the person of Christ. Christ Himself, however, consecrated His Body at the Last

Supper and gave it to others to eat, and hence just as the power of consecration of Christ’s Body belongs to the priest, so too does the administration of that Body to the faithful. Since the priest is mediator between God and the people, as he offers God the people’s gifts, so too must he give the people the divinely sanctified gifts. ”412

The sinful priest still has the power to consecrate, though he should not draw near to the altar: “The priest does not consecrate by his own power, but rather as Christ’s minister, in whose person he consecrates this sacrament. The priest does not cease to be Christ’s minister simply because he is evil, since the Lord has both good and bad ministers or servants, as Christ Himself says, ‘Who, then, is the faithful and prudent servant,’ etc.; then, ‘But if that wicked servant says to himself,’ etc. . . . As the Apostle says [1 Cor 4:1], ‘thus should one regard us: as servants of Christ,’ and later ‘I am not conscious of anything against me, but I do not thereby stand acquitted’ [1 Cor 4:4]. He was therefore certain that he was Christ’s minister, and yet was not certain that he was just. Hence, a man can be Christ’s minister even if he is not just. This belongs to Christ’s excellence who, as true God, is served by both good and evil, since all things are ordered by His providence for His glory. Thus it is clear that priests, even though they might not be good, but rather evil sinners, can consecrate the Eucharist.”413

In question 83 alone Saint Thomas uses the word “God” and variations of it some forty times, but I think that what we have seen should suffice.
