MYSTERY - MIRACLE

“Mysterium fidei”414

ROMAN MISSAL

The Eucharist is the “miracle of miracles”415

POPE LEO XIII

What comes about?

In the Eucharist, Almighty God brings about a mystery and a miracle: it is a mystery because it contains truths and realities that are beyond the understanding of all created intellects, even if we could somehow put them all together. It is a miracle because it exceeds what can be done by all created powers, even if we could somehow combine them together.

Thus God, by His power, changes the entire substance of bread and wine into the entire substance of the Lord’s Body and Blood, and He attaches what comes inseparably linked with them.

A. Mystery

Citing Eusebius, Saint Thomas says, “‘As the Body that Christ had assumed would be taken from their eyes and raised to the heavens, it was necessary that He would consecrate the Sacrament of His Body and His Blood for us that day of the Last Supper, so that the One who once offered Himself as our ransom might be forever adored in mystery.’”416

Later, citing Saint Augustine, “‘The Savior, in order to more

A gloss reads, “Speaking of this sacrament, the Apostle [1 Cor 11:21] says, ‘one goes hungry while another gets drunk,’ and the gloss comments, ‘This refers to those who, after the celebration of the sacred mystery and the consecration of the bread and wine. . . . ’ ”418

Likewise, Saint John Chrysostom, “commenting on the words, ‘immediately blood and water flowed out’ [Jn 19:34], says, ‘since it is here that the sacred mysteries have their origin, when you approach that tremendous chalice, draw near as though you were to drink from the very side of Christ.’ Hence, the Lord Himself says, ‘This is my blood of the covenant, which will be shed on behalf of many for the forgiveness of sins’ [Mt 26:28].”419

The Angelic Doctor raises the following objection: “Occasions for error should be taken away from men, as Isaiah says ‘Remove every obstacle from my people’s way’ [57:14]. However, some have erred by thinking that Christ’s Body and Blood are only mystically present in the sacrament, and so it is unsuitable to use the formula ‘Mystery of faith.’”420 He answers it by saying, “‘Mystery’ is used here not to exclude the truth of the content, but rather to show that it is hidden: Christ’s Blood is hidden in this sacrament, and Christ’s Passion itself was hidden in figures in the Old Testament.”421

He insists even more on the difficulty: “Earlier it was said that Baptism is ‘the sacrament of the faith,’ and that the Eucharist is ‘the sacrament of charity.’ Thus, this formula should say ‘of charity’ and not ‘of faith.’”422 Thomas refutes this objection by saying, “‘Mystery of faith’ is used referring to the object of faith, as it is only by faith that the real presence of Christ’s Blood in this sacrament can be maintained. Likewise, Christ’s passion justifies by faith. Baptism is called ‘the sacrament of faith’ because it is a declaration of faith. It is called ‘the sacrament of charity’ inasmuch as it signifies charity and is the cause of it.”423 “The Savior, in order to more vehemently extol such a lofty mystery, wanted to affix it in the hearts and memories of the disciples”424 at the end of His life.

B. Miracle Part of the miracle is the power given to the accidents:

“Some of the actions of bread follow from it because of its accidents, such as to affect the senses. Such operations remain in the species of bread after the consecration, since these accidents remain.

However, some operations follow from bread either on account of the matter, such as being converted into something else, or on account of the substantial form, such as the operation that is a consequence of its species, for instance, that it ‘sustains the human heart.’ Such operations are found in this sacrament, though not because the substantial form or matter remain, but rather because these operations are miraculously conferred on the accidents themselves.”432

“Hence, just as Divine power allows the sacramental species to exist without a substance, so it is also an effect of Divine power that the accidents can act without a substantial form, since the action of every form, substantial and accidental, depends on God as first agent.”433 “The passage to a different substantial form is not done by a substantial form directly, but rather mediately through the active and passive qualities which act in virtue of the substantial form. This instrumental power is conserved in the sacramental species, just as it was before [the consecration], by the divine power. Thus, it is possible for them to act instrumentally in the change of the substantial form, and in this way they act outside of their species, not by their own power, but rather by the power of the principal agent. ”434 “Since it doesn’t seem reasonable to say that there is something miraculous in the sacrament that isn’t caused by the consecration, and the consecration doesn’t imply the creation or return of matter, it seems better to say that in the consecration, the dimensive quantity of bread and wine are miraculously made to be the first subject of subsequent forms, a characteristic which is proper to matter. As a consequence, everything that pertains to matter is in turn given to dimensive quantity. It follows that everything that could be generated from the matter of bread and wine, if it were present, can be generated from its dimensive quantity, not by a new miracle, but rather by the power of miracle already brought about. ”435 “Even though there is no matter [in the species] from which a thing may be generated, dimensive quantity takes the place of matter.”436 “Those sacramental species are accidents, though they have the act and power of substance.”437 “The dimensive quantity of bread and wine retain their own nature, and they miraculously receive the power and properties of substance; hence they can change into both, that is, into substance and dimension.”438 “Food nourishes by being converted into the substance that is nourished. It was said that the sacramental species can be transformed into a substance that is generated from them. Hence, they can be transformed into a human body for the same reason that they can be changed into ashes or into worms. Thus it is clear that the sacramental species can nourish.

Thus, the senses attest that the position of those who say that these species do not really nourish as if they were changed into the human body, but rather refresh and strengthen by means of some sensible immutation, just as man is strengthened by the smell of food and inebriated by the smell of wine, is clearly false. Such refreshment cannot long sustain man, whose body, on account of continual wear, needs to be restored. A man could be sustained for a long time, however, if he consumed large quantities of consecrated hosts and wine.

Nor can the position be maintained of those who say that the sacramental species nourish by means of the substantial forms of bread and wine which remain after consecration. This is not only because these substantial forms don’t remain . . . but also because it is not the act of the form to nourish, but rather the act of matter, which receives the form of the one being nourished while losing the form of nutrient. This is why nourishment is said to be unlike at first, but like at the end.”439

“Once the consecration is completed, ‘bread’ can be said to be in this sacrament in two ways. First, it can be said of the species, which retain the name of the previous substance, as Gregory said. Secondly, Christ’s Body itself can be called bread, since it the mystical bread ‘come down from heaven.’ Therefore, Ambrose, when he says, ‘this bread doesn’t come into the body,’ is taking bread in the second sense, since Christ’s Body is not changed into man’s body, but rather refreshes his soul. He is not, therefore, speaking of bread in the first sense.”440 “Even though the sacramental species are not those things of which a human body is composed, they are nevertheless converted into it. ”441 “The sacramental species, although they are not substances, have the power of substances.”442 “The place where Christ’s body is is not empty. Nor is it, properly speaking, filled with the substance of Christ’s Body, since this isn’t present locally. . . . Rather, it is filled with the species of the sacrament, which must fill the place either according to the proper nature of dimensions or miraculously, just as they subsist miraculously like a substance .”443

By God’s power, the accidents are miraculously present without a subject: “It must be granted that the accidents in this sacrament remain without a subject, something that can be done by God’s power.”444 “The corruption of the species is not miraculous, but rather natural. Nonetheless, it presupposes the miracle of consecration, in virtue of which the being that the accidents had in their subject before the consecration is preserved without the subject. It is comparable to a blind man who miraculously receives the gift of sight, and from then on sees naturally.”445 “In a decretal Pope Innocent III says that ‘the accidents themselves appear to affect the wine, since, if water were added, it takes up the flavor of wine. It happens that sometimes the accidents change the subject, just as the subject changes the accidents. Clearly nature yields to miracle, and power acts above and beyond habit.’ This, however, must not be understood as though the accident, numerically the same that was in the wine before consecration, is later something added to the wine; rather, the change comes from action, since the remaining accidents of the wine retain the action of substance, as was said above, and thus they act on the liquid by changing it.”446 “In this sacrament the consecration of the matter consists in the miraculous change of the substance, which only God can do.”447

Saint Thomas raises the following difficulty: “No created power can perform a miraculous work; only divine power can do so, as was said above. However, the change of bread and wine into Christ’s Body and Blood is no less miraculous than the creation of the world, or the formation of Christ’s Body in the virgin’s womb. Such things could not be done by any created power. Hence, neither can this sacrament be consecrated by any created power of the aforementioned words.”448 He resolves it in this way: “No creature can perform miracles as the principle agent, but a created agent can do so instrumentally, just as the touch of Christ’s hand healed the leper. It is in this way that the words of consecration change bread into Christ’s Body. In Christ’s conception, however, by which His body was formed, it was impossible for any part of His body to have the instrumental power of forming that body. Similarly in creation, there was no subject which could receive the instrumental action of a creature. Thus, there is really no comparison between them.”449

“The fire of desire within us, received from the burning coal, that is, this sacrament, will burn away our sins and give light to our hearts, so that by participation in the divine fire, we might be enflamed and made 450

like God.”

SAINT JOHN DAMASCENE

Dear Reader:

God and His Most Holy Mother very much want to give you the grace proper to this sacrament-sacrifice which is actual refreshment of spiritual sweetness: this is the enjoyment of the incomparable taste of this supersubstantial Bread and that inebriating Blood, an enjoyment that the Angelic Doctor reminds us of many times:

“This sacrament not only has the power to give the habit of grace and virtue, but also to move to act, because ‘the love of Christ impels us’ [2 Cor 5:14]. Hence, it is by the sacrament’s power that the soul is nourished; by it the soul is delighted and inebriated, as it were, by the sweetness of the Divine goodness, as is read: ‘Eat, friends; drink! Drink deeply, lovers!’ [Sg 5:1].”451

“As was already shown, the effect of this sacrament is not only an increase in habitual grace, but also an actual refreshment of spiritual sweetness. Hence, while Christ’s grace did not increase upon receiving this sacrament, He nonetheless had a certain spiritual delight at the new institution of this sacrament, as He said, ‘I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you’ [Lk 22:15], which Eusebius says refers to the new mystery of the New Testament which Christ gave to His disciples. Thus, Christ ate His Body spiritually and also sacramentally, inasmuch as He received His body in the sacrament, a sacrament which He both understood and prepared. However, He received it differently from others who receive it both sacramentally and spiritually, for these receive an increase in grace and need sacramental signs in order to perceive the truth of what they receive.”452

EPILOGUE

“As was already said, the effect of this sacrament is not only the reception of habitual grace or charity, but also actual refreshment of spiritual sweetness. This sweetness is impeded if someone approaches this sacrament with their mind distracted by venial sins; however, the increase in habitual grace or charity is not destroyed.”453

“The one who approaches this sacrament with venial sin eats spiritually, but this is in habit, and not in act; hence, such a one gains the habitual effect, but not the actual one.”454

“Baptism is not ordered to the actual effect, that is, the fervor of charity, as this sacrament is. Baptism is spiritual rebirth, through which the first perfection, that is, the habit or form, is acquired. This sacrament, however, is a spiritual eating, which brings an actual delight with it.”455

This “certain spiritual delight” grows even more because the Eucharist, the sacrament-sacrifice, is the guarantee, source, and pledge of eternal salvation, as Aquinas repeatedly insists:

“Two things must be considered in this sacrament: the sacrament itself and its effect. Its effect [res tantum] is the unity of the mystical body, without which there can be no salvation, since there is no entering into salvation apart from the Church, just as in the time of the flood there was no salvation outside of Noah’s ark, which is a symbol of the church, as Peter says [1 Pet 3:20-21].”456 “As the Apostle says, no one can be saved without faith in Christ’s passion: ‘whom God set forth as an expiation, through faith, by his blood.’ [Rom 3:25]”457 “This presence is also in accord with Christ’s charity; it was on account of His charity that He assumed a true body of our nature for our salvation.”458 “Those who do not receive this sacrament can still benefit from it as a sacrifice, inasmuch as it is offered for their salvation. This is why the Canon of the Mass says, ‘Remember, Lord, your servants and all gathered here, whose faith and devotion are known to you. For them, we offer you this sacrifice of praise or they offer it for themselves and all who are dear to them: for the redemption of their souls.’”459 “It is clear, as was already said, that everyone has the obligation to eat this sacrament at least spiritually, since this means to be incorporated into Christ. Spiritual communion, however, includes the

EPILOGUE

will or desire to receive this sacrament sacramentally. . . . Hence, no one can be saved without the desire to receive this sacrament. However, this desire would be in vain if it were not fulfilled when the opportunity presented itself. Thus it is clear that man has an obligation to receive this sacrament, not only because of the Church’s precept, but also because of the order of the Lord Himself, who said, ‘Do this in memory of Me’ [Lk 22:19; 1 Cor 11:24].”460

“This sacrament is celebrated in memory of the Lord’s Passion, and is received for the soul’s salvation.”461

“This sacrament contains the entire mystery of our salvation.”462 It is the “Bread of eternal life and the Chalice of everlasting salvation”463

The Eucharist is the very heart and center of all the means “by which we obtain our salvation.”464

Cedit quippe natura miraculo, et virtus supra consuetudinem operator.’ Hoc tamen non est sic intelligendum quasi idem numero accidens quod prius fuit in vino ante consecrationem, postmodum fiat in vino apposito, sed talis permutation fit per actionem.
